.BY TE DEEP: DEEP BEA." A SONG. The winds blew loud with angry roar, Dark, black clouds, in the sky did lower, The foam-capped waves, like mountains tower, Oa the deep, deep sea. The sailors struggle the ship to save. But the good ship sank 'neath a seething wave, Each sailor found a watery grave. In the deep, deep sea. A form of a maiden, young and fair, With wild, sad look, and dishevelled hair. To the rocky shore, in grief, cloth repair, By the deep, deep sea. . The waves beat high. and break at her feet, As she murmurs a song. so low and sweet, She Lightly goes her lover to meet. By the deep, deep sea.

" 0 come to thy lonely love again, Come back to me, o'es the stormy main. And ease this burdened heart of pain, . By the deep, deep sea. I wait for thy coming, night by night, I watch for thy ship to come in sight. Thy coming, will make my sad heart light." By the deep, deep sea. The echoes answer, from rocky cave, Thy lover sleeps, with his messmates brave, At rest, at rest, in their watery grave In . the deep, deep sea.
One night, a form arose from the S. And the maiden cried—" He calls for me, I go to my love, at peace to be. In the deep, deep sea." J. G. PICICERWILL.

- MIGHT HAVE BEEN. What might have been, but ne'er can be, Alas t with saddened brow We think of lovely drooping flowers, That might have flourished now. Ot many a struggling mattyr, Who passed in youth away; Yet might have lived to share with us Each bright and happy day. Of many homes when meagre want With dull and sunken eye. Reigns on :n savage tyranny. Until her victims die; And evrn in life's budding time, The cheeks are Fad and thin, That might, with childhood's merry laugh, Have made the woodlands ring. And many a weeping orphan, Neglected and alone, To whom the world is harsh and cold, An object of its scorn, Around whose early infancy, Affection's flowers were shed, That might have bloomed more beautiful, As youthful years had fled. And many desolated hearths, For ruthless death may show The silent mourning agony Which from bereavements flow. Yea, many are with sorrow teruAled. Whilst joyful birds may sing, 'Who might have lived in full delight. And hailed the welcome spring. O'er natures full of sympathy What shades of gloom are cast; Affection often basely wronged Must sorely die at last. And truthful hearts have been betrayed, And noble lives undone, That might for human happiness Have greater conquests won. Warrington. B. KENTON.

You can tell a merciful farmer, says the Detroit Free Tress, as soon as he stops his team at a post. He takes the blanket off his wife's lap and spreads it over the poor horses. A stranger in St. Louis, thinking he recognised his coat on the back of a pedestrian, shouted, "Stop Thief !" and about thirty of the inhabitants suddenly disappeared down a side street. A young bride read Mother Shipton's prophesy for the first time the other day. "Just my luck !" she exclaimed, throwing down the paper. "Here lam newly married, and now the world's coming to an end." A meditative man was roaming through an anatomical museum, and came across the skeleton of a donkey. " Ah! " he said, in reverential awe, as he adjusted his green spectacles," we are, indeed, fearfully and wonder- fully made!" Gilhooly hired a pony the other day to take a little exer- cise on. He got all the exercise he wanted, and as he limped to the edge of the sidewalk to rest himself, a kind friend asked him: "What did you come down so quick for ?" "What did I come down so quick for? Did you see any- thing up in the air for me to hold on to ?" A New Orleans paper thus discourses :—" If men are the salt of the earth, women are the sugar. Salt is a necessity, sugar is a luxury. Vicious men are the salt-petre ; hard, stern men the rock salt ; nice family men the table salt. Old maids are the brown sugar, good-natured matrons the loaf sugar, pretty girls the fine pulverised white sugar." Dean Swift, in preaching an assize sermon, was severe . open the lawyers for pleading against their conscience. After the dinner, a young counsellor said some severe things against the clergy, and ided that he did not doubt, if the devil were to die, a parson might be found to preach his funeral sermon. "Yes," said Swift, "I would, and give the devil his due, as I did his children this morning." Apropos of the pronunciation of Arkansas recently antho- ,:sisil ui the Legislature of that State, an Arizona paper claims that that ::'rritory offers more obstacles to a "tender foot" in the matter of ',‘-s2 ,swonunciation of local names than any other territory or State in the ral.oll. It instances , Gila, Iluachuca, and Hualapai, which, it says, are pro- nounced, Heeher, Wor-chu-kar, and Wol-lar-pie. Tun HEAD OF Tun HOUSE.—During the taking of the census, a shoemaker's wife, who was asked if she was the head of the family, answered that she was not. On being questioned as to what relationship she bore to that person- age, she replied, with contempt, "The heed o' the hoose, Map ? Wey, ax waddent be the heed. Aa's better nor the heel. Aa'e the neck if thoo wants to knaa ; for aa can torn the heed onyway ax like!" A sailor coming on board drunk was met by the Duke of Fdinbnrgh, who, addressing him sternly, said—. What do you mean, sir, by being drunk onboard ship? I won't have it, sir. And I hear besides that you've been drunk on shore. I won't have it, sir." The inebriated tar steadied himself for a moment, and, looking the duke full in the face, hic- cupped up—. Well, if a man mayn't get drunk on shore, and mayn't get drunk aboard, where is he to get drunk, your Rile Highness ?" Sam Johnsing (coloured) was up again yesterday. "Whit brings you here this time," asked the Recorder. "De plice- man, Bah; de same what brung me heah last time." "I mean what did you do ?" "I was jess passin' a grocery store, when I struck my head agin a ham what was hangin by de dore. I tuk de ham down to put it somewhares whar it would be safe from folks huatin' dar brains out agin it, when de fast I knowed a p'liceman tried to get de ham away from me; and bekase I wouldn't let de ham go, he jess brung me along too."—American. LITTLE WHEEL AND BIG WHEEL. Bays the big waggon wheel To the little waggon wheel, " What a difference between us I see! As our course we pursue. Can a small thing like you Keep up with a great thing like me Says the little waggon wheel To the big waggon wheel, "You are larger, I own, my good friend; But my quickness supplies What I want in my size, So I keep in the front to the end." A LITERITSUN'S TROUBLE.—Last week, young Reepitup was out with a team all one afternoon. When he drove into the stable, oh! but the man was mad. "Look at that hoes," be wailed, "look at that hosed Ain't a dry hair on him, an' he's nigh ready to drop. That's a pretty lookin' way to bring in a boss. Nice man, you are, to let a good hose to !" Young Keepitup was fairly astonished. "Man alive," he yelled, picturing his amazement in his voice; "and what did you expect when I hired him? When a horse is costing me an even five dollars an hour, he's got to keep moving, you understand. When lam paying out more than eight cents every minute, I can't afford to let no horse lean up against a feed box while he figures out the oat crop of the United States for 1880. I did my level best to keep my whip arm warm, and then I couldn't get mOre than 4 dollars 25 cents an hour out of him. I didn't hire the horse to rest him. Now, if you had only charged fifteen cents an hour, I would have had the horse fed every thirty minutes while I was out, and I would have rocked him to sleep in my arms, wrapped him up in blankets, and hauled him back to the stable myself. That is the difference, you see, Mr. Silkeracker." And he went away, while Mr. Silkcracker stood looking alternately at the money and the horse, think- ing it all over.—Toronto Mail. ALEXANDER lI.—E. C. Grenville Murray writes as follows of the late Czar in the Continental Times Alexander softened and generally improved with age, excepting that in one notable particular he remained a Sar- danapalus to the last. Like the wiss -t of kings, he was the slave of women. But in his youth be was somewhat harsh, Or, it would be luster to say, at times. The times in ques- tion were those following upon a too gay breakfast. The Czar liked champagne, and was apt to be sulky when the effects of that treacherous wine were passing off. Once be must needs go and inspect a school rather too soon after breakfast. The children and their parents were mustered to receive him, but the Czar refused to be pleasant. He found fault with everything, and acted altogether rather queerly. A terrible urchin whispered in an audible undertone to his mother, 'The Czar's drunk.' Alexander heard, and was sobered' in an instant by the shock. But he could not con- trol his anger. 'That child's sick,' he said aloud, pointing to the boy, let him be taken to a hospital, and after that to a madhouse.' The young scapegrace was hurried out of the room, but nothing was done to him, and naturally the Czar was careful to make no inquiries after him. He was not the man to injure any one in cold blood. In old age—for he was old at fifty—he foreswore sack and lived rationdlly, if not ideally. His greatest pleasure was then to take lorg unattended except by a sin rambles foot, gle friend. His health was not good, and he tried all sorts of Cures,' es- pecially the grape cure, which almost anticipated the work Of the assassin. If one must divide kings into good and bad, as in story books, a I exarder IT. decidedly belonged to the former category. If sovereigns, however, could be placed as in the schools at Oxford one would give hint a .rerond rises. with the additional remark that it was a very creditable second."

HOW MANY EGOS WILL A HEN LAY IN A YEAR?—This will depend on breed, age of hen, food, and other circum- stances. You may rely on this—Fifteen hens laid within ' the year 2,280 eggs, and ereared 30 chickens. The number of eggs was 152 each, and that iva capital average even for a non-brooding sort. An experienced egg farmer informs us that hens will lay from 100 to 180 each in a year, and he aims at 200. A foreign authority has said of hens generally that the ovarinm of a fowl is composed of 600 ovules, or eggs; therefore a hen, during the whole of her life, cannot lay more than 600. He distributes these—he says that he distributes them—over nine years, as follows :-Ist year, 15 to 20 (our hens do far better !) • 2nd year, 100 to 120; 3rd year, 120 to 135; 4th year, 100 to 11,5; and afterwards less than half as many.—Agricultural Gazette. FARMERS' Tnorrmas.—Farmers will be glad to learn, on the authority of Lord Thnrlow, that their troubles are nearly at an end. In a letter to The limes his lordship says :—" The seed is not only in the ground, but has been got in under the most favourable conditions. Sunshine in May is all the young plants need, and meteorologists en- courage us to expect it Fat cattle maintains its price, and there is a larger head of cattle in the country than there has been for several years; while the undoubted failure in sheep on most cold and wet, though fortunately by no means on all, soils, with perhaps an occasional over-draft at hirf banker's, is all that remains to remind the British farmer of the damp and dismal years he has gone through." Ameri- can competition, too, will soon cease to be formidable, Lord Thurlow thinks. LAND PRODUCE IN THE UNITED STATES.—Authoritative statistics recently complied show the extremely productive character of certain states in the American Union: It ap- pears that a group of states with less than a third of the , population-of the country produces five-eighths of the corn supply of the United States. These states are Ohio, In- diana, Illinois, lowa, Missouri, Kansas, and Nebraska, and the following figures will show the enormous progress which has been made within the limits of a generation. The corn growth of Ohio in the year 1859 was 73,543,190 bushels, and in 1877 97,000,000 bushels. The produce of Indiana had gone up in the same period from 71,588,919 to 96,000,000 bushels; Illinois, from 115,174,777 to 260,000,000 bushels; lowa, from 42,410,686 to 156,000,000 bushels; Missouri, from. 72492,157 to 103,000,000 bushels; Kansas, from 6450,727 to 98,000,000 bushels ; and Nebraska, from 1.482,080 to 38,000,000 bushels. In 1877 the product of these seven states was nearly 850,000,000 bushels, and of all the rest of the Union only 494,548,000 bushels. Mr. J. R. Dodge, of the United States Agricultural Department. says that the wheat surplus is produced entirely in that portion of the country north and west of the Ohio river, in the cen- tral area lying between that river and the lakes, and the Alleghany and Rocky Mountain ranges, and in a smaller area on the Pacific Coast. There has been a great transfer of corn production from the South to the West, so much sa that while in 1849 15 Southern States produced 50 per cent. of the corn product of the country the whole of the South now produces only one-third. This change is partly due to the increase in the cotton product of the South, but it is said that the South may yet regain its supremacy in the corn culture. It is a surprising, yet authenticated, factthat in 15 years the production of wheat and barley in the United States has trebled; that of corn, cotton, and tobacco has more than doubled: oats have increased by two-thirds, po- tatoes have nearly doubled, and hay has increased by nearly one-third. -

BOOKBINDERS' METHODS.—CaIf is really what is called the skin of the calf, prepared by the process called by tan- ners " tawing." The na4ral colour of the skin is a very light drab, but it turns darker in time, and becomes a light brown. The uncoloured skin is pleasant enought to the eye, and is used in the peculiar style of binding called "Law," since it is commonly used for law books. The skin, how- ever, can be dyed any colour, and it has then an agreeable appearance but as the mordants used in the dyeing are apt to attack the leather, and cause it to go more than it other- wise would have done, the best style of decoration for calf is the colouring of the natural skin by the binder. There are various ways in which this is done. It may be sprinkled wholly or in part. This is effected with a hog's-hair brush, dipped in a strongish solution of copperas (protosulphate of iron) in water ; the brush is scratched with the nail, and the small drops are allowet to fall upon the cover, or upon a portion of the cover, the rest being protected by a covering. The copperas mixing with the tanning left in the skin pro- duces a kind of ink, and so darkens the spot where it falls. Considerable variety may be caused by protecting various portions of the cover in patterns, and graduations of the colouring can also be effected. Another mode of colouring is called French catspaw. This is produced by dipping a piece of wool, or similar substance, in the colouring matter, and dropping it on the cover, thus forming a more or less regular seriee of patches of dark colour. A third style of ornamentatimi " tiee ca:f." Ttn prodqss by which this curious style of ornamentation is brought about is almost as remarkable as the marbling the edges of the leaves. The cover, which, of course, must not be too thick, is bent upwards away from the book into the form of a channel. This is held slanting, at an angle, say, of thirty degrees ; it is then sprinkled with pure water pretty freely, -until the various spots begin,to. run into one another' and to find their way down to the central channel; and thys` to fall off the cover. At this moment some very finely powdered copperas is dropped on the wet spots, and allowed to run down with the stream. Where the water is sufficient it carries off the iron, but where the leather is only damped it allows the colour to sink down into the skin. Some little experi- ence and neatness of hand are required to give the desired effect, and to produce on the two covers a corresponding effect, which, however, should not be too closely alike.— CasselPs_Technical Educator, for May. OrIR HOltE LlFE.—What a little world home is to those whose lives are almost wholly spent there ! It is a little world to all of us, but a great world to them—just their world, with its affection, its agitations, and alas! its ani- mosities; with its occasions of joy and sorrow, and, alas! of sin. What scope for the working of the good spirit, and, indeed, of the evil too; room enough for the practice of every piety—and of every impiety. Piety we define ac- cording to its derivation, that which is holy. This is the tree. But "the tree is known by its fruit," and the fruit of the tree, "the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, tempe- rance." There is a very different list, in which we M;atatich undesirable companions as " hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like." But we will not speak of this evil inven- tory; we want yours to furnish only the good. And is there any place on earth better suited for their display than home? And is there anything on earth that would make home more beautiful than these virtues and graces of character and life? Would to God we all liked always to show such "piety at home !" For if we did, all fathers would be fatherly (which they are not) and mothers motherly; brothers would never fail to be brotherly (as they now do fail), nor sisters sisterly. We want the root as Well as the fruit. If the fruit be home virtues, the root is home holi- ness, even as the flower is the home happiness. The root is holiness, the root is Christ. Show holiness at home, show Christ at home. Let the Christian husband show Christ by beginning and never failing to continue family prayers. We said the archetype of our English home is to be sought , among the patriarchs; well, wherever they went we read, "there they builded an altar and called on the name of the Lord." Let the Christian wife show it by gathering her children, even if she cannot get her husband. and praying for him if she dare not pray with him. Let Christian sons and daughters show Christ, not only by the sweetness of their lives, but by words for Jesus, and work for him. And let Christian servants show their piety by diligence and faithfulness, not with eye-service, but as in the sight of God. So, one and all, learn the divine secret, how to " show piety at home." But what is the Secret? The secret is Christ, and the Spirit of Christ. To show piety you must have it to show, and to have it you must have God first; you must be " partakers of the Divine nature," partakers of Christ. "Be filled with the Spirit," and you will be "filled with the fruit of righteousness." Let heaven be your home and your home will be heaven. Then will our home life be Christlike, when to us to live is Christ, and we shall show piety at horne.—Sunday at Home for May, TIIROAT IRRITATION.—SOrerIesS and dryness. tickling and Irritation. inducing cough and affecting the voice. SCIENTIFIO NOTES. A bronze statue of Pante has lately been set up in the square of the Celltligilde France, this being the quarter in which he lived when in Paris in 1302. Mr. Millais's new painting, "Little Miss Gamp," has just been added to the collection in the Graphic Gallery. This picture is the companion to the same artist's "Cherry Ripe.' According to the Atheneum, M. Michel Rossi states that accumulations of fire-damp are accompanied by faint sub- terranean noises which the Microphone indicates with much sensibility. By grating sounds this instrument proclaims the escape of gas, and M. Rossi argues that this, added to barometric warnings, would forewarn the superintendents of mines and consequently prevent explosions. osluanr Spectrum." Boyle, of Hull who has a large colllection of his own, is engageo upon a Bibliography of the literature relating to Swedenborg and the New Church from the publication of Swedenborg's first work in 1709 to the present time. It will include also non-denominational writings by New Church authors, and works written in opposition to the teachings of the New Church. The book is expected to be published within the current year, and will contain notices of nearly 6,000 separate publications. At Milan some frescoes have been discovered, in a house now the property of the municipality, and which the I chronicler Torn, writing in 1672, declared to have been de- I corated by Bernard Luini. In the course of some repairs the frescoes came to light, but the connoieseurs declare that they are not the work of Luini but of Cesar daSesto, another pupil of Leonardo da Vinci. The pictures include the seven days of the Creation and other scriptural and allegorical sub- jects. They are being removed to the Gallery of the Brera. Experiments have been carried on in the works of Messrs. David Moseley and Sons, of Manchester, for some time past with a view to finding a material which will re-place carbon for telephonic transmitters with advantage. It is stated that the experinagots have been entirely successful, and that the material has t een patented in this country and abroad. Mr. Preece has expressed a high opinion a the invention and will read a paper on the subject at an early meeting of the Society of Telegraph Engineers. M. Pauchon, a French observer, has been making experi- ments on the germination of beans. He states that black or violet seeds absorb more oxygen than white or yellow ones, though a more rapid germination is observed in the latter. Carbonic acid is said to be exhaled in greater quantity from white than from dark seeds. "The more frequent and pro- nounced pigmentation of the seeds of Northern lands is, therefore,' says M. Pauchon, "a favourable circumstance for the growth of these organisms under the peculiar light. conditions to which they are subject." INLAYING WOOD BY PRESSITRE.—A method of inlaying wood by pressure has been recently introduced. It consists in glueing a veneer of the wood to he inlaid over the com- mon wood, and placing a zinc "stencil" plate with the pat- tern cut out of it over the veneer, then subjecting the whole to the softening action of steam and the pressure of two powerful cast-iron rollers. These rollers crash the stencil into the veneer, and the underlying veneer into the common wood. The stencil is then withdrawn, and the embedded . portion of the veneer is planed down till the inlaid surface • is perfectly smooth and even. 1 ST. ALBAN'S ABBEY.—Sir Edmund Beckett has entered ' into a contract for the rebuilding of St. Alban's Abbey, ac- I cording to his design. It will be remembered that when, some time ago, protests were made against the destruction of the old front, Sir Edmund took his stand upon the faculty I, which the weakness of the local ecclesiastical authorities had allowed him to obtain, and defied all comers. That faculty does not give him any power to alter the great west window, which Sir Edmund has declared it is his intention to replace by one of his own. ,There is, therefore, still a chance, if those responsible for the 'wilding will, in turn, take their stand upon the faculty, that the inside at lean of the west part may be saved from serious disfigurement. —Atheneum. A Pocxxx PULSE-WESTER.—The condition of the pulse has from the earliest times been held as a valuable aid to the diagnosis of disease ; but until the sphygmograph, or pulse-writer, was invented, the pulse was only read by the finger of the doctor, which varies in sense with different men and at different times. Moreover, it can at best only tell whether the pulse be soft or hard, quick or slow, jerky or languid, regular or irregular; it cannot analyse the beats and detect any variation in each of the elements which make up the total movement. The pulse-writer, on the other hand, enables the pulse to record its own movement, for all to see, so that the physician can distinguish at a glance where it differs from the healthy or normal pulse. Hitherto this most useful instrument has been little used, except in hospitals, owing to its cumbrous nature. The same objection does not apply to the pocket sphygmograph of Dr. Dudgeon. This apparatus is only two and a half inches long by two inches wide; it weighs only four ounces, and is therefore well adapted for private practice. The movement of the pulse is taken up by an adjustable spring pressed upon it, and communicated by a system of delicate levers to a stylus, which traces a line upon a band of smoked paper, kept running by a small clockwork. A dial indicates the pressure put upon the spring, which may amount to five ounces. The smoked paper runs through the instru- ment in ten seconds, so that the number of pulse-bea s per minute can be reckoned by multiplying the number on the tracing by six. The patient's name, and disease, the date, and so on, may also be scratched upon the paper, which, on beini dipped in a quick-drying varnish, can be kept for re- ference and comparison. This little apparatus magnifies the movement of the artery no less than fifty times. It can be applied to the patient in any posture, and gives its auto- graph of the pulse almost as quickly as a physician can feel it with his finger. THE TIDE-PREDICTOR.—Sir William Thomson has in re- cent years turned his inventive genius aud great scientific i knowledge to the improvement of the instruments of navi- gation. As Sir George Nitres said recently, he has bettered all the "three L's" of the sailor—namely, the lead, the log, and the look-out. His patent compass is now recognised to be the compass of the future,his pressure lead and sounding apparatus by pianoforte wire is being introduced into many mail steamers and men-of-war, while his mode of making light-houses flash their distinctive names according to the Morse telegraphic code is also proving its superior worth. But Sir William has besides turned his attention to the measurement of the tides, an important matter for an insular and seafaring nation like ours, and has invented three most ingenious apparatus for the purpose. These are the Tide- gauge. the Tidal Harmonic Analyser, and the Tide-predictor. The Tide-gauge registers the actual height of the sea-level, by means of a float- actuating a pencil marking a running band of paper; the Harmonic Analyser substitutes brass- work for human brains in calculating out the different ele- ments which compose the whole tidal rise and fall; while the Tide-predictor, as its name implies, does nothing less than predict for any particular port, and for any future year, not merely the times of high and low water, but the position of the water-level at any instant of any day of the I year. The action of the instrument is to draw curves of the tides at that port; one year's tides being, in the latest form devised, run off in 24 minutes. The elements of the tide at the port in question furnished by the Harmonic Analyser are the data upon which the Predictor operates. The details of the apparatus are too complicated for de- scription here; but we may mention that the different ele- ments of the tide are combined by means of a fine steel wire I or cord passing round several pulleys corresponding to these' elements. One of these Predictors has already done good service in predicting the tides or the Indian ports as given in the volume of Tide Tables for 1881. PnerrOnttaPnic PHOTOMETRY.—A promising application of photography to precise measurement of phenomena of light has been recently tried by M. Janssen. The method is advantageous, in that photography reveals the action of the extremely weak luminous and ultra-violet rays; but the chief advantage lies in the permanence of the results, as against the fugitive nature of ordinary photometric com- parisons, which, too, require the simultaneous presence of the two light sources. The various amounts of metallic de- posit on the photographic plate cannot well be weighed, so M. Janssen measures by the degree of opacity produced. I His photometer consists of a frame with sensitised plate, be. which Is passed at a known rate of uniform motipe a shutter having a slit. If this slit were rectangular, a uni- form shade would be produced on the plate; but by making it triangle he obtains a variation of shade, decreasing from the side corresponding to the base of the triangle to that corresponding to the apex. It is further proved that the photographic deposit does not increase as rapidly as the luminous intensity. Now, to compare the sensibility of two plates differently prepared they have merely to be exposed successively in the frame under like conditions, and the points where they show the same opacity being compared to the points of the triangular slit corresponding to them, the ratio of the apertures at those points expresses the ratio of sensibility. Thus the new gelatino-bromide of silver plates are proved to be 20 times as sensitive as the collodion plates prepared by the wet process. Again, to compare two luminous sources, they are made to act successively on two similar plates in the photometer, and the points of equal shade in the plates indicate, as before, the relation sought. M. Janssen has compared the light of the sun and some stars on these principles, preparing from the former " soladleales" (with uniform degradation of shade), under exactlgwdeter- mined conditions as to sensitive layer, time of solar action, height of the sun, (tn. Circular images of stars are obtained by placing a photographic plate a little out of focus in the telescope, and a series of these got with different times of exposure, are compared with the scales obtaineif rem sun- light. M. Janssen will shortly make known some of his re- sults.

--- The strike of workmen on the Grand Trunk Railway has terminated. And now trichinm have been discovered in fish. What a blessing if some one could find the dreaded insect in whiskey I If your wife is small of stature you have this philo- sophic consolation—viz., that of all the evils you have chosen the least. Rebecca Webber has been sentenced at Portsmouth to seven days' imprisonment for throwing a cat into a copper of boiling water. A telegram from New York states that there is every- where a good prospect of an unusually large wheat crop in th United States. An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth seems to be the Nihilist motto. The Czarina is now threatened if the female conspirators are executed. Can a man be rightly said to be "on his legs" again when he has sold his horses and carriages for theoweet sake of his creditors and is compelled to walk? More Philadelphians have gone to jail for illegal prac- tices at thepolls, but political machines always are supplied with duplicates of their various parts. When a man produces a thousand and one vehement argu- ments to prove that he is innocent, your verdict ought to be "Not guilty; but he mus'nt do it again." A correspondent writes that a marriage was to have taken place the other day at a chapel near Ribchester, but theßegis- trar failed to appear, and the ceremony had to be deferred till next day. The election for president of the Congregational Union', for the coming year took place in London, on Monday, with the following result :—The Rev. Mr. M`Farlyen, T 26; Dr.' Parker, 449. The net quantity of iron and steel rails manufac-, hired in the United States during last year was 1,461,837, , tons, being 31 per per cent in excess of the amount pro- duced in 1879. A large number of trees were destroyed by fire on Sunday, in Cookridge and Horsforth woods, near Leeds. Some 28 acres of ground suffered. The fire is supposed to be due to the careless use .of matches. At Wednesbnry, on Tuesday, Thomas Hodkinson, cashier, in the employ of Messrs. Rigby and Sons, ironmaeters, Wed- nesbury, was committed for trial for embezzling £5O, and also for falsifying their books. The Leicester Liberal Club on Saturday pissed a resolu- tion protesting against Mr. Bradlaugh'sexclusion from Parlia- ment, and thanking Messrs. Gladstone and Bright for sup- porting the rights of constituencies. Obstinate people, who are perfectly sure that they are right and equally sure that every one else is wrong, remind us of the man who searched for his drowned wife by going up the stream because, as, he said, iFte was a woman who never went with the current. A large meeting was held on Tuesday in the market place, Leicester, to protest against the attack on representa- tion by the refusal of the House of Commons to admit Mr. Bradlangh, and to urge the Government to push on the 0,q13s Bill. At a Church Defence meeting, a petition was adopted against any alteration in the law to admit an Atheist to Parliament. Edward Keeling, 18 years of age, was charged at Salford Police Court, on Monday, wityli stealing money and some articles from'two houses where be had obtained accommoda- tion on representing himself to bee Roman Catholic student "in difficulties." It was stated that ha had been going about the country defrauding people in this way. He was com- mitted for trial. Some residents of Union City, Id., have formed what they call the "National Marriage Dowry Association," the object of which is declared to be to encourage lawful wed- 'lock, to promote economy, to endow homes and to make married life the end and the aim of the rich and the poor alike. It promises to pay a dowry in three classes, $l,OOO, $2,000, and $3,000 respectively. Six men were remanded at Carmarthen on Saturday, charged with a dastardly outrage. Late one night they visited a wooden tenement near Carmarthen, inhabited by a bedridden woman, 80 years old, her widowed daughter, and child. After beating the inmates, the ruffians fastened the doors from the outzide, and set the house on fire. The build- ing was completely distroyed, and the inmates escaped with great difficulty, being severely bruised and burnt. A New Hampshire farmer recently agreed to sell his farm for $2,000, but when the day came he told the expectant purchaser that his wife was in hysterics about the trade, and "lie guessed he'd have to back out." The purchaser complained, and finally asked how much more would induce him to sell. "Well," replied the thrifty son of the granite state, "give me $250 more, and we'll let her cry." A, the Newcastle-on-Tyne Police Court, theßey. Matthew Rennie, a clergyman of the Church of England, who has been suspended, was brought up on a charge of being drunk and assaulting a police-sergeant. It was proved that the prisoner conducted himself badly in the streets, and used violence to all policemen who went near him. The I magistrates sent him to prison for a month, without the op- tion of a fine. Catherine Marshall, aged 14 years, the Strathaven fasting girl, has passed her eighteenth week without food. She was visited last week by several medical men, who acknowledge themselves puzzled by her case. A proposal to send her to Glasgow Infirmary was declined as incurring great risk. When offered milk she buret out crying, and it was hours before she recovered from the excitement. Numerous remedies are suggested from all parts of the kingdom. It is announced that the Duke of Portland has appointed the Rev. H. Cavendish Browne to the rectory of Bredon, in the diocese of Worcester, vacant by the death of the Rev. H. Fitzgerald. The rectory is worth about £3,000 a year, and there are about 1,500 persons living in the district. Mr. Browne's name does not appear in the English "Clergy List," but he is described as " son of the Dean of Lismore and brother of Baroness Bolsover." Probably he is one of the Irish clergy who "commuted " under the Disestablish- melt Act. In reply to a clergyman who asked for information re- specting the Lord Chancellor's views as to Mr. Bradlaugh, Lord Selborne writes that he has never had the slightest difference, or tendency to difference, with his colleagues in the Government upon any question relating to Parliamen- tary oaths or affirmations, whether connected or not with Mr. Bradlaugh's case. While sharing the clergyman's feel- ings about Mr. Bradlaugh's publications, he considers equal justice is due to Christian and infidel. An estate agent brought an action against a hairdresser in the Liverpool County Court, on Monday, to recover damages for loss which he had incurred from having his throat cut "in the defendant's shop. The plaintiff was being shaved by an assistant when the defendant, passing quickly along, accidentally raised the assistant's arm, and caused the infliction of a wound about one-eighth of an inch deep and two inches long. The jury thought that the wound was worth £1 Is. 4d., and, in giving a verdict for this amount, they added a protest against being brought into court to settle so" trumpery a case." SPRING MORNING COSTUME.—A very neat costume may be made of washing sateen with striped trimmings. This costume comprises a long princess polonaise and walking skirt. The polonaise fits closely to the figure, and on either side of the buttons a striped band starts from the neck, and is continued all round the edge of the polonaise. The cuffs on the coat-sleeves are also of the striped material, as well as the turn-down collar and waistband. The short skirt is edged with kitting 12 inches deep, and a border of the striped goods a little distance from the edge. The polonaise is draped at the sides, so that the heading of the flounce is quite invisible. To make this costume, 12 yards of sateen will be required, and two yards of the striped sateen. Ai small skull bonnet of straw, the crown surrounded with flowers, is worn with this costume.-3frs. Leach's Family Dressmaker. • Mr. Bradlaugh has issued an "appeal to the people,>, in which he calls for support in his endeavour to take his seat in the House of Commons. He chlirges the Conservative party with wishing, under cover of his case, to jeopardise the Irish Land Bill. Addressing a meeting at Woolwich on Saturday, Mr. Bradlaugh said that some of his opponents were heirs to the "rotten pensions" which be had attacked, and that, and not his irreligion, accounted for their disin- clination to allow him to enter the House. None but the constituency of Northampton had the right to judge him. All that "rascality and calumny" could do bad been done to oppose him. This quarrel was not his, it was the question of the right of the people to elect their own can- didatea. A ROMANTIC STORY.—Thetween twenty and thirty years ago, a gentleman named Taylor, residing near Haslingden, died, leaving considerable property in London and else- where. Unfortunately no will could be found, though what purported to be a copy of it was produced, by which the property is left—one-half to the Messrs. Isherwood, of Has- linden, and the other half to John Seddon, of Bolton, and their heirs. One of the ladies is dead, but the other (now Mrs. Walton) is living. Seddon died some years ago in the workhouse. Recently an old pocket-book has been found in the clothes left by Seddon, which, it is thought, affords a clue to the long-lost will. The book contains an entry to the effect that Seddon had proceeded to London and lodged .a will in the office of a solicitor there, to be detained till called for. A few months afterwards Seddon died. A Bolton solicitor has now gone to London to make search for the will,and if it be found it is thought there will not be much difficulty in securing the property, which is of the estimated value of £4,000,0001 and the heirs to which are all in humble circumstances. MARRYING A COUPLE AGAINST THE PARENTS' WISHES.— that a scene witnessed at a church There is every probability in the neighbourhood of Burnley on Sunday week was but the prelude to a dispute which may bring the principal characters before the public in other capacities. It seems that the objections of the father of the aspiring youth, although the latter was stated to be only 18 years of age, failed to influence the mind of the clergyman, for last Sun- day morning he united the young couple in the bonds of holy matrimony, the youthful husband having, it is re- ported, taken out a license without the knowledge and con- sent of his parents. His father heard of the circumstance as the ceremony was taking place, but only arrived at the church gates in time to see his son returning with his newly- made wife leaning upon his arm, while another son was in- dulging in a caper to give vent to his merriment at the spectacle presented. The affair has caused a good deal of amusement, and the liveliest anticipations are entertained of the future proceeslings which, it is already asserted, are certain to follow this interesting episode. The disappointed lather has, it is said, consulted an ecclesiastical lawyer, and has written to the Bishop of the diocese on the subject of a prosecution. The quality of Rartley's Damson is unequalled.—ADVT.

Lord Palmerston at on resigned, resigned, receiving, however, before resigning intelligence of the triumph of his Chinese policy, and of the capture of Canton by the British troops. This unexpected fall of Lord ralmerston is not without its lessons. When the Session commenced in 1858 he was still strong and apparently a stable Minister, with an un- broken majority at his back, and with an amount of confi- dence all but unimpaired. A few weeks passed away, and this British Minister par excellence falls from power,because he advocated what to the majority of the House seemed an anti-British policy—because, with fatal fascination, he fixed his eyes on the great Boa Constrictor of the French until he was ready to yield to that Imperial Dictator one of the most clearly-cheriled rights and most deeply-rooted prejudices of the British people. In the sudden and unexpected fall of this petted and, perhaps, honoured idol of the people, we have another proof of the impossibility of opposing the strong will of Parliament and the omnipotence of Public Opinion.

EPISCOPAL TACT.—A new church was about to be opened by the bishop, and a number of neighbouring clergy were invited to be present at the ceremony. Arrangements had been made for the clergy to walk into the church in prows- sion in surplices the bishop last. The procession was formed, all was ready, when the rector came to the bishop, sayicg, " All will be spoilt, two clergy are come in black gowns; they declare they will wear them in the procession. They are come for the purpose of openly showing their evangelical principles." The bishop replied, "All will be well; they will go in surplices." The rector assured the bishop that this was impossible, and that any remonstrance he might make would only cause a disturbance. The bishop, after again re-assuring the rector, said to the clergy, who were formed two and two, "Gentlemen, are you ready ?" and re- ceiving a reply in the affirmative,he stepped along the rank, and accosted the first blackgowned clergyman with "Good morning, Mr.—; will you have the kindness to read the First Lesson for us this morning?" Then, passing to the second, with the request that he would read the Second Lesson; the two fled to find surplices, and the procession went into church with the two clergy clad as the others.— Life of Bishop Wilberforce. • J PRIME MINISTERS. LORD PALMERSTON. The General Election which followed the Dissolution of Parliament in 1857 possessed at least one noticeable feature peculiar to itself. There were not, as is usually the case, any burning questions upon which the country was invited to record its decision. The issue before it was simply restricted to that of confidence or want of confidence in Lord Palmerston. The adverse vote recorded by the House of Commons on his Chinese Policy had led his Lordship to accept the sarcastic advice of Mr. Disraeli. "Let the noble lord," said Mr. Disraeli, in replying to LE rd Palmerston at the close of the debate; "Let the noble lord, who complains that he is the victim of a conspiracy, not only complain to the country—let him appeal to it." And Lord Palmerston did appeal to the country, for he shrewdly imagined that the mistakes involved in the Chinese War were not sufficient to destroy the faith of the British people it, their Chief, who had at all times borne aloft the red-cross shield. The gal- lantry with which Lord Pahnerston had stepped forward in 1855 to take the helm when the violence of the storm seemed about to overwhelm the vessel of State, and when divided counsels paralysed the hands of its chief officers—the energy with which, undeterred by the perils of the crisis, he held on his course, and finally the success with which, in an alliance with the French Emperor, he brought the good ship into a secure haven, had laid in the gratitude of the nation the basis upon which had been reared a reciprocal affection which no temporary misunderstanding could overturn. And when it became known that peace had been just concluded with Persia on terms favourable to both beligerents, many imagined that his policy in China would end right, and that the opposition thereto arose in the main from opponents who were anxious to oust Lord Palmerston from Downing- street in order to make room for themselves. This feeling was considerably strengthened by the tidings of alleged cruelties perpetrated by the Chinese, and which reached this country on the very eve of the Election. Moreover, Lord Palmerston had won golden opinions from the Evangelical party of the Church of England by his appointment of Evangelical bishops and clergymen to the vacant bishoprics anklivings. He was eulogised by them as the true Protes- tant—" the Christian Premier," "the man of God." And though the secret of these appointments was perhaps to be found in his lordship's relation to the Earl of Shaftesbury, yet he seemed to have been guided mainly in his ecclesiasti- cal patronage by the desire to advance really good men rather than to elevate persons noted only for secular learning or for mere Churchmanship. With all these influences in his favour we are not sur- prised to find that at the election he had it all hiS own way, while the party which had condemned his Chinese policy, the great party which had procured the repeal of the Corn Laws, which had enabled Peel and Gladstone to carry out their excellent financial measures, which had inscribed on their banners "Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform," were smitten hip and thigh and turned hors de combat all along the line, Richard Cobden, John Bright, Milner Gibson, and others were all rejected by the constituencies which had previously elected them by large majorities, and that, too, without any change of opinion on their part. In all 189 new members were returned to Parliament with a working majority in favour of the Government far beyond their utmost expec- tations. "Our elections will be over this week," wrote the Prince Consort to the Dowager Duchess of Coburge on 9th April. "The Ministry have gained 24 counties and 20 boroughs, and the Apostles of Peace have been turned out by the people neck and crop. Not because the people do not love peace, and are not greedy of money, but because they love their own importance and their own honour, and will not Submit to be tyrannised over by the peace-at-any-

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT,
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

THE BEACONSFIELD MONUMENT.—EarI GRANVILLE moved that an "address be presented to her Majesty praying that her Majesty will give directions that a monument be erected in the collegiate church of St. Peter, Westminster, to the memory of the late Right Hon. the Earl of Beacons- field, K.G.. with an inscription expressive of the high sense entertained by the House of his rare and splendid gifts, and of his devoted labours in Parliament and in great offices of Slate; and to assure her Majesty that this House will coa- cur in giving effect to her Majesty's most gracious mes- sage." He said he must confine his observations within narrow limits, for he was not the man to give any biographical sketch of a man so well known as Lord Beaconsfield, or to enter into an analysis of his policy or political actions, and for him to give arty approval of those remarks would have an appearance of insincerity which would be as displeasing to their Lordships as it would not be creditable to himself. It was, however, impossible for anyone to deny that Lord Beaconsfield played a great part in English history, that he pAsessed rare and splendid gifts, and that he achieved by his own strong individuality, without the aid of any adventitious circumstances, the great personal success to which he attained—Lord SALISBURY seconded the motion, and paid high tribute to the benefits which had resulted from the policy of the late Earl of Beaconsfield.— The motion was agreed to. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mormar. Turns AND THE FRENCIL—In answer to Mr. Otway, Sir CHARLES DILEB said it was quite true that French troops had landed at Biserta. The Military Attache at Paris in- formed him that the number was about 3.000 men. The Bey of Tunis had protested against this act. His Highness stated in his protest that he continues to be at peace with France, and the French Consul continues to hold relations with the Bey. Of course, such an act might or might not be taken as an act of war, according to the pleasure of the Bey.

Mr. DILLON.—Mr. RumEn stated that he was informed that Mr. Dillon was seriously ill. He did not think the Government could agree to release him if he was likely to repeat that for which it had been necessary to imprison him. THE FRENCH TREATY.—Replying to Mr. Slagg, Sir CHARLES DUKE stated that the Government had been officially informed that the new Faench general tariff was promulgated on Saturday. The commercial treaties with France would expire on the Bth ef November. Her Majesty's Government had urged on repeated occasiens the commence- ment of negotiations on the subject of these treaties. The French Government had always made the sa,ne reply, namely' that they could not proceed with the negotiations till the Bill to establish a new tariff had passed its second reading. THE BEACONSFIELD MEetontet.—The Speaker having left the chair, Mr. GLADSTONE, before a crowded House, moved an address to the Queen praying her to give direc- tions that a monument be erected in Westminster Abbey to the memory of the late Earl of Beaconsfield, with an in- scription expressive of the "high sense entertained by the House of his rare and splendid gifts, and of his devoted labeurs in Parliament and in great offices of State," and assuring her Majesty that the House would make good the expenses attending the same. In submitting this proposal, the right hon. gentleman earnestly entreated that it might not be made the subject of contentious or lengthened argu- ment. He admitted, however, that the position of the House was in some respects peculiar, for he did not know that it had ever happened that a Parliament which was in sharp antagonism to a particular Minister had been called on to accept a proposal of this kind; but he recommended it in the first place as a tribute to one who had sustained a great historic past, and done things which were written on the pages of Parliamentary and national history, and in the nest place because these things had been done with the full authority of the constituted organs of the nation, and of the nation itself. Upon neither of these points was there the smallest room for doubt. The career of Lord Beacons- field was in many respects one of the most remarkable in our Parliamentary history. His name was associated with a great Constitutional change in connection with the Parliamentary franchise, and with great European arrangements which were settled under the Treaty of Berlin. For thirty years he had in that and the other House led a great party, and for many years sustained the office of Prime Minister. It was not his intention to draw a his- torical portrait of Lord Beaconsfield, but it would be a satis- faction to himself to allude to some of his great qualities. For Example, besides his intellectual powers, Lord Beacons- field possessed others not less remarkable. These were his strength of will, his long-sighted persistency of purpose, his nower of self government, and last, but not least, his great Parliamentary knowledge. There were also those strong elatufdorltihkee sympathies with his race, for the sake of which lie wa's readytoadrmi ski tahtiiseup,ompurlaGriltaydsatnedu Gladstone influence; nhce l e aa 1 sentimentw ''Y of f strength of Lord Beaconsfield's sympathies with the brother- hood of the men of letters. Lastly, there was his profound, devoted, tender, grateful affection for his wife. In conclud- ing his speech, the right hon. gentleman expressed a wish to record his own firm belief that in all the judgments delivered by Lord Beaconsfield on himself he was , neyer actuated by any personal antipathy.— Sir S. NORTHCOTE, in seconding the resolution, remarked that if he could contemplate for one moment that the pro- posal would not meet the unanimous acceptance of the House. he should still have the consolation of feeling that a monument had already been raised to the memory of Lord Beaconsfield of a far higher character than any that could be carved in stone or marble, and that was in the speech the House had just heard. That speech had been both nobly expressed and still more nobly conceived, and in that tribute to the memory of a sharp political opponent by one with whom he had been in the very severest of political contests they had a record which was honourable not only to the speaker and to Lord Beaconsfield, but to the British Heim of Commons. As one who had a very large share of intimacy with Lord Beaconefield for many years, he could entirel c confirm the statements of the Prime Minister, that in all his contests there was nothing in Lord Beaconsfield's mind or spirit that was unworthy of a generous antagonist. They were asked to do honeur to a man whose rare gifts they all admired. Although Ids obsequies had been private, yet England was there. The hearts of the people turned towards Hughenden on that day. and whether or not a monument was erected to him, the name and the fame of him they had lost was secure in the memories of English- men, and would never perish. Mr. LABOUCHERE. who presented himself amid cries of " Agreed," was of opinion that unless such a resolution met with general concurrence from all sides of the House, it would be better that it should not be put, and there were on his side of the House many who thotreht that the Premier in the matter of generosity had done too much. They admired the perseverance and energy which enabled Lord Benconsfield to attain the highest position in the State, as well as his tact and urbanity in leading a great political party, and they fully shared in the regret of his [friends at his loss. But the question wee, whether a monu- ment was merited, not only by the character of the man, but by his Policy as a Minister, and that the country had con- demned. With regard to precedents for the present proposal, Mr. Labouchere maintained that there were none to show that a public monument had ever been voted to a Prime Minister unless he had had a majority in the House who con- sidered that he bad perforneed great and signal services to Ids country. Thinking, then, that the grounds stateEi in the resolution were not sufficient to entitle Lord Beaconsfield to this public memorial, and that the country had no reason to be grateful for anything that Lord Beaconsfield had done, the hon. member moved that the Chairman leave the chair. The amendment was seconded, without remark, by Mr. CAINE, and after some words from Mr. Arthur O'Connor, delivered amid the noise of much talking, the House divided. and the amendment was rejected by 380 votes against 54.—0 n the proposal to put the main question, Mr. BIGGAR asked Mr. Gladstone whether, in view of "this large numerical majority." he intended to proceed with a resolu- tion which. if it had any value, should be passed unani- mously.—Mr. GLADSTONE said he certainly did intend to Press the motion.—lt was then put from the Chair, and not being seriously challenged, was carried without a division. —On the return from the division lobby, Sir A. GORDON explained that he had accidentally voted in the wrong lobby, having intended to vote against the amendment.— Between 30 and 40 members left the House when the divi- sion was called. THE limn LAND BILL—The House then resumed the debate on the Irish Land Bill.—Sir 3. Houma condemned the sweeping change the bill wonld effect in the relations of landlord and tenant as gross confiscation. If such conces- sions were made to the Irish people when they clamoured for them, they mustalso be given to the people of England and Scotland when they demanded them.—Mr. BRIGHT con- tended that the Irish land system bad completely broken down, and the main cause of this was the insecurity of tenure, to which he traced also the poverty and discontent of the country. The present condition of things could not be left untouched—either we must go forward or backward; and what the Irish tenants asked for was not a wild plan of confiscation, but a measure which would give them adequate security in their holdings at an adequate rent. As to the "fairt orfer clause, he anticipated that over the greater pm Ireland rents would continue much as they are, but the parties would be put in an improved relation to each other, and would be able to agree with each other without going into court. The other clauses would give the tenant that security which the tenant required, and though they did certainly make many concessions to the tenants, they were accompanied by This, he said safeguards for, the landlords' interest. complexity ortheincidentally, WOS one of the reasons of the measure, As to compensation to the landlords, his answer to that was that nine-tenths of the houses, barns, fences. and-land of Ireland were the general cultivation of the produce of the tenants' e labour, and not of any xtoenditure by the bill he the land- lord. On the purchase naturally laid most stress, because of usses were possible by a stroke to convert& he held that if it oc- cupiers into owners it would be a longreetep towards making -fourths of the Ireland prosperous and contented. step emigration, he concluded by claiming for the bill remarks on -eerie worked fairly and with energy it would 11 that if it be a blessing a the Irish people.—Sir R. CROSS, deiticising the bill and pecially the purchase clause, asked what better position is tenant who had borrowed the whole purchase m euld be in under the State than under his landlord.— °n"' se debate was then adjourned, on the motion of Mr. te.w. _
HOUSE OF LORDS.—TumsDAT.

The quality of Hartley's Dams, is unequalled.—Anrr. At the annual sleeting of the Council of the Liberation Society, held on NVedneaday, a resoltition was passed ap- proving of the principle of giving a member ot Parliament the option of taking the oath or affirming, and urging the friends of religious freedom to assist the Government in passing the Parliamentary Oaths 8111. At the public meet- ing held in the evening Mr. W. E. Baxter. M.P., who pre- sided, said Nonconformists hod abandoned all watchword- like" toleration" and " removal of disabilities," and wonlc be content with nothing less than absolute ecclesiastical equality. But the land question not only in Ireland but hi England came first in order, and time was on their side.
