div.p: THE EXAMINE],, SATURDAY. MAY 14, 188 L

reference made to the Transvaal question by Mr. Gladstone in his letter to Mr. Tomkinson, who was then the Liberal candidate for West Cheshire, said the real responsibility for the unhappy events that have taken place, was to be found in the Midlothian speeches of the ?rime Minister, and in the appointment of Mr. Courtney to an office in the Govern- ment. The reversal of the annexation was unwise, and he warned the Government that there was no peace in the settlement that had been agreed upon.—The Earl of KIM- BERLEY, in reply, said he might perhaps have attached a little more importance to the charge that the insurrection was promoted by Mr. Gladstone's speeches, were is not for the fact that the Boers were also represented as being , encouraged by Mr. Courtney's appointment, which, unfor- tunately for the truth of the allegation, did not take place till after the insurrection had broken out. He was far from being without hope that the Transvaal war would be brought to a lasting settlement, but he was aware of the difficulties which beset the question. He was certain that the policy I which Lord Carnarvon initiated could not have been main- tained. Whether the policy of the present Government would be more successful he would not pretend to predict, but the motives were as good as those which actuated the noble earl, and he trusted that the chances of success might be somewhat greater.—The Duke of ARGYLL also defended the course taken by the present Government on this ques- tion, whilst Lord BRAROURNR expressed the opinion that it was likely to lead to most disastrous results.—After a few words from Lord STANLEY of Alderley, the subject was allowed to drop.
'gousic OF COMM&S.-TSIIIISDAY.

FEES FOR Lcint, BPACONSI. lELD'S MONUMENT.— MACDONALD gave notice of his intention to ask the Finan- cial Secretary to the Treasury whether it WAS true that the fees payable to the Dean and Chapter of Westminster Abbey In connection with the monument to Lord Beaconsfield would amount to f. 400; and, if so, whether these fees would I be the private epolument of the Dean and Chapter, or, if not, for what purpose they were levied. THE SCOTCH VOLUNTEERS.—MI. CHILDERS announced that the Queen had authorised him to say that a review of the Scotch volunteers would be held at Edinburgh some time between the 20th and 31st of August. THREATENED ABDICATION OF THE PRINCE OF BULGARIA. —Replying to hon. members, Sir CHARLES DILKE said he regretted to state that the reports with regard to a political crisis in Bulgaria, and the rumoured intention of Prince Alexander of resigning, were conirmed by information received by the Government. VACCINATION AND PAUPER CHILDREN.—Mr. DODSON, in reply to Mr. Hopwood, as to whether boards of guardians had power to enforce the vaccination of children born in a workhouse without obtaining the consent of the mother upon admission, said in his opinion vaccination could not be enforced if the mother objected. MR. Dm.ox's Artussr.—Mr. GrAusrorrE declined to set aside the Irish Land Bill to allow facilities for the discussion of Mr. Dillon's arrest. MR. BRADLAUGH'S EXCLUSION—Si I STAFFORD NORTHCOTE raised the question, upon Sir W. Lawson's notice of motion in the Bradlaugh case which was set down for discussian on Friday night whether it was competent for a member to move that a resolution adopted and acted upon by the House was "illegal."—The SPEAKER thought it would have been better if Sir Wilfrid had moved in regular form that the resolution be rescinded, but he regarded the matter as one of privilege, and as such he did not think the member for Carlisle had forfeited his claim to have it considered. He advised that the expression " illegal " should be with- drawn.

THE Irma LAND BILL—Mr. GLADSTONE expressed a strong hope that the debate on the Irish Land Bill would be concluded on Monday evening.—The debate on the second reading was resumed by Mr. Straw, who, in an effective speech suggested that an addition should be made to the rent clause, stipulating that the work done by the tenants in improving their holdings, should in no way be calculated against them in the valuation of their land. The hon. member also urged that the case of farmers who were paying too high a rent to be able to make up arrears should be considered by the Government, and that the county court judges should be instructed to postpone the necessity for their payment until the courts to be estab- lished by the bill could look into the cases, and offer some relief. Mr. Macnaghten, the Conservative member for An- trim county, announced that he should vote for the second reading of the bill. The debate was continued by Mr. Lit- ton, Mr. Redmond, Sir J. Ramsden, Mr. Mitchell Henry, and other members. In the course of a discussion as to the position of the Land Bill, it was stated that there were still 40 members waiting to speak upon it.
PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.

IMPORTANT MEETING. The monthly meeting of the Pr;scot School Board was ‘held on Monday evening, at the Clerk's offices, Derby- street, Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P., presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. T. P. Hewitt, J. Sanders, W. Goldsworth, and J. J. Brown; with Mr. Henry Cross (clerk). THE FEVER EPIDEMIC: CLOSING OF THE BOARD SCHOOLS. The CHAIRMAN remarked that the meeting was called a week earlier than usual at his suggestion in a great measure, set' with Mr. Wycherley's approval, to decide whether the ' schools should, after the annual examination, which was I fixed for the 12th and 13th instant, had taken place, be closed for a three weeks' holiday; and a further holiday to be given in the first week in August. There had been a great ! falling off in the number of children attending the schools, consequent upon the prevalence of scarlet fever in the town, and it struck him that it would be a very good thing to close the schools, after the examination had taken place, for a three weeks' holiday. In face of the fever they could not: compel parents to send their children to school, and they I could not expect to have any respectable attendance. At the end of three weeks the disease might not be so bad; it we improving row he believed. The CLEM( said he thought it was. The CHAIRMAN further observed that the teachers and scholars would have the same length of holiday, though at a different time. In answer to the Chairman, Mr. LIGHTFOCrT, the school- master, said the school year terminated on the 30th April. There were 239 names on the register in the boys' depart- ment, and the average attendance for the year was 166 as against 171 in the previous year. The total number of at- tendances was less by over three thousand, the numbers being—last year, 74,6:37 • this year, 71,371; decrease, 3,296. Mr. BROWN remarked ;hat the falling off.in the attendance would not be the result of fever, because he understood that of late there had been a higher average. Mr. LIGHTFOOT said that since Mr. Lloyd became the attendance officer there had been an increase in the at- tendance. The falling off took place during the first six or eight months of the school year. In September last the average attendance had sank down to 143. The average last week was 170. Mr. Hewerr did not consider it was fair to charge Mr. Miller, the former attendance officer, with the whole of that. There was a great deal of poverty in the town at that time. The CHAIRMAN said that had nothing to do with it. Mr. liewery said it might not have anything to do with it theoretically, but it seemed to him that at one time the Board did not press the attendance the same as they did at the present time. He did not say Mr. Lloyd failed to do his work, but he did not wish to be unfair to Mr. Miller. The CHAIRMAN did not say it was Mr. Miller's own fault. His health had been bad, and he was unable to do the work. In answer to a question, Mr. LIGHTFOOT stated that the attendance had decreased from 201 on April 4th to 170 at •the end of last week. Mr. SANDERS thought it very strange that the fever did not affect the poorer children in the town—he meant the children attending the Yew Tree Poor Schools. There were not more than three cases in those schools. For himself, he believed children would be better in school than out of it. If they were left about the streets all day they got mixed together, and went into houses where they were more likely to take the disease than if they were at school. Parents thought their children caught it at school. Mr. GOLDSWORTH said they were liable to catch it either inside or outside. The fever was very contagious, and it was wonderful how it could be carried away in the clothes. Mr. SANDERS asked if the doctors had recommended the closing of the schools. Mr. BROWN thought they could not do anything more than move in accordance with the first portion of the notice I convening the meeting, and close 'the schools for three I weeks after the examination. It seemed to him to be a common sense view of the matter. They must take all the precaution they could, and. perhaps by the end of three , weeks there would be more confidence in the minds of the ' public and of parents. He therefore moved that after the examination the schools be closed for a three weeks' holi- day, to be followed by another week in August. He did not think they could act more prudently than by'so doing. The CHAIRMAN agreed with Mr. Sanders that the children would be quite as safe in school as rambling in the street or ' at home. If they could isolate them it would be different, but they could not do that. They played about the streets and went into these houses, and were quite as likely to spread the epidemic by staying at home as going to school ; but the Board could not force parents to send their children to school in face of the epidemic. Mr. GOLDSWORTH said that Dr. Hall, the medicel officer, had drawn ups pl %card giving information and directions I to parents and others as to what should be done in eases of 1 fever breaking out in their houses. Looking at the matter , from every point of view, he thought it would be as well to' close the schools for three weeks after the examination, and be had great pleasure in seconding Mr. Brown's motion. Mr. BROWN remarked that in all cases of fever no child affected should be sent to school for six weeks after it had recevered, and three weeks was quite as little as they could agree to. Mr. LIGHTFMT, in answer to a question, said that up to that morning there were 14 who would not be present at the! examination owing to there being fever at their homes. The motion was then put to the meeting and unanimously agreed to. Mr. Leorrreoor asked if the children were to be supplied , with oranges, as formerly, when they separated for the I holidays. Mr. BROwN: I should think oranges would be a very good thing from a sanitary point of view. It will have the effect of bringing up a few who might otherwise stay away. It was understood that oranges would be distributed as usual. In reply to the Chairman, Miss DIME, the mistress of the girls' school, said she was afraid they would have a very poor inspection this year. The CHAIRMAN: How many will you be able to present? —Miss Dann: 68. The CHAIRMAN: How many did you present last year 7- 74. The CHAIRMAN: Will all those 65 children appear before the inspector ? Miss DUKE: Well, the best of them say they cannot come,l as they have fever in the house. The CHAIRMAN: How many will you lose on that account? Miss DUKE: Half a dozen, at least. I would suggest that j those who cannot attend be examined with some other school not yet inspected. The Crternalaw : And forget all their " cram ? " (Laughter.) Miss MCGREGOR, mistress of the infants' school, said she , would be able to present 64 for inspection, as against 71 I last year. THE CLOSING OF THE GIRLS' SCHOOL WITHOUT AUTHORITY. The CHAIRMAN (to Miss Duke): I omitted to mention one thing. You did not tell us last Easter Monday that you had closed your school in the afternoon, and closed it without the authority of the Board? Miss DUKE explained that it was owing to a mistake. She was under the impression that the schools were closed on Easter Monday, but on reference to her log-book she found that it was not so. She mentioned that on a former occasion Mr. Lightfoot closed his school without authority. Mr. Lioirreocrr denied, emphatically, having done any such thing. Mr. Elxwerr did not think the matter should be carried further, and accordingly it was allowed to drop. ATTENDANCE OFFICER'S REPORT. Mr. Was. LIAM), the school attendance officer, reported that since the last meeting he had visited the parents of 93 I children who had been absent or irregular in their atten- dance at the various schools in his district, lie had served notices upon 14 parents, representing 19 children, the same being due on the 18th instant. He had, as directed at the last meeting, visited the parents of those children attending! the girls' school, and who resided outside his district, the result being that two or three et them, who were reported to have been sick, had been got IS school again. The sum- mons which he was instructed to take out at the last meeting bad not, as yet, been disposed of, owing to the want of a magistrate. The medical gentlemen whom he was requested to see had kindly consented to sign the certificates of sick- ness of cases in which they were engaged, free of charge. One of the gentlemen stated that if it was a case which he had only casually attended, and it required a visit or examination, he could not sign the certificate free of charge. The CHAIBMAN said he had seen one of the doctors, and he said he would give the officer any verbal information, but did not think he should be asked to give certificates for nothing. If the officer got a form printed, he (the doctor) would sign it for him. During some further conversation on the report Mr. Hewtrr said it seenvel to him to be almost impossible for Mr. Welch to discharge his duties as school attendance officer of the Prescot union, with satisfaction, even if he devoted the whole of his time to the office. Mr. GOLDSWORTH was of a similar opinion. The CHAIRMAN observed that it was his idea that the officer for the union should be officer for that district. Mr. GOLDSWORTH: Yes; or make arrangements with the officer of this Board to see to the whole of the New Brighton district. The subject then dropped. THE HOUGHTON.STREET SCHOOL.—LETTER FROM THE EDUCATION DEPARTMENT. The CLERIC read the foleowing letter, dated April 30th, which he had received from the Education Department : " Sir.—The Prescot Church of England school was accepted in 1871, as providing efficient school accomodation in this district. The school is not, however, in receipt of annual emnts, and has not, since that time been inspected. My lords ire of opinion that if the school is still to be reckoned as providing accommodation for the district, application should be made by its manager for its recognition as a certified effi- cient sclaool under section 48 of the Elementary Fducation Act, 1876. lam directed to enquire whether your Board can furnish their lordships with the name and address of the vntleman through whom they might correspond with the trustees of the school on the aubject.—l have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant, P.Crame." At the request of the Chairman, the CLERK read the sec- tion refevred to. Mr. Hewirr observed that according to that the school could have to be re-formed. The CHAIRMAN remarked that the school was certified in 1871, and had not since be3n inspected, and it should be. Mr. BROWN asked if the clerk had in any way or shape i replied to the communication.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIESDAY.

PETITIONS IN FAVOUR or Mn. BRADLAVGII.—Mr. LanorcrtEau presented a petition signed by 7,000 inhabitants of Northampton, and an armful of petitions from other towns, praying that Mr. Bradlaugh may be allowed to take his seat at as early a date as possible.—As Mr. Labouchere made his way to the table, he was met with some cries of "Too late" from the Opposition benches.—Colonel Maxms put an ob- jection that was not competent to present petitions alter five o'clock.—The petitions were received. THE BASIITOS.—Mr. GRANT DUFF stated that the Basutos hid not, so far as the Government knew, rejected the terms of peace offered them, and that the new Ministry at Cape. town had not repuiliated British sovereignty. THE FRENCH AND Tams.—Sir C. DIME made a brief statement on Tunisian affairs, in the course of which he stated that there was some reason to suppose that the French Government had protested against the sending of Turkish ships of war to Tunis but the Foreign Office had not received any communication from the Porte, and therefore had no authentic information on the subject. CHARGES AGAINST METHODIST MINISTERS. Mr. FORSTER, in reply to Mr. Birt, said it was true that three Primitive Methodist ministers had been summoned before the magistrates at Belfast, and committed to prison for 14 days in default of paving a fine for singing hymns and con- ducting a procession through the streets. A notice of appeal had been lodged, and he would, therefore, not pronounce any opinion in favour of the legality of the conviction. He would remind his hon. friend, however, that very fre- quently crowds and processions in Belfast caused serious disturbances.

------- TEE Cotermitous DISEASES Acre.—ln reply to 'Mr. Hop- wood, who called attention to the case of Elizabeth Burley, who threw herself into Dover Harbour to avoid the prosecu- tion of the police under the Contagious Diseases Acts, Sir WE. HARCOURT said that his attention had been called to the letter in the Daily News in which the girl declared her innocence, and was supported by the evidence of Mr. Alfred Dyer, who had made inquiries into the case. If the girl's story was true he acknowledged that a great wrong bad been done to her, and she was entitled to the utmost sympathy and redress. In previously answering the question he had been bound to go upon the information before him. He slid not complain that such cases should be most carfully watched. His own duty was a delicate one, since, on the one hand, he mustprotect innocent women against molesta- tion, and even women who were justly suspected from harsh treatment ; and, on the other hand, he had to protect the police from being deterred from the proper execution of their duty under the Acts. He had directed an exhaustive investigation to be made into the matter by all the means at his disposal, and if his hon. friend could suggest any further mode of examining into the matter, he should be most happy to consider his suggestions. (Hear, hear.) MR. BRADLAUGH AND THE OATH: ANOTHER SCENE.— Upon Mr. Parnell rising to put a question, Mr. BRADLAUGH advanced to the bar of the House, and repeated his demand to take the oath.—The SPEAKER at once ruled that the recent order of the House that Mr. Bradlaugh should with- draw below the bar was still in force, and he called upon the junior member for Northampton to retire.—Mr. BRAD- LAUGH respectfully submitted that the order was illegal and refused to obey it.—At the request of the Speaker, the Sergeant-at-Arms conducted Mr. Bradlaugh below the bar, but he immediately returned and reiterated his refusal to obey.—The Speaker having appealed to the House for fur- ther instructions, after a short pause Sir S. NORTHCOTE moved that the Sergeant-at-Arms do remove Mr. Bradlaugh from the House until he shall engage no further to disturb the proceedines of the House.—Mr. GLADSTONE stated that he did not hold himself bound to resist the motion, and he certainly should not encourage any such resistance in others. His own belief was that Mr. Bradlaugh had a right to come to the table, and holding that belief he did not think it would be consistent, or becoming, or dignified, or of service to the State that he should move that Mr. Bradlaugh be taken from the table. He pointed oat that it was one thing to obey an order of the House and another to undertake to guide the house by making a motion—Mr. LAROuCIIRRB wished to know the precise meaning of Sir S. Northcote's proposal, and the right hon. Baronet replied that members in the position of Mr. Bradlaugh were regarded as incom- pletely returned, and it had been held that they were entitled to seats below the bar, and the object of his motion was that the hon. gentleman should not come within the door of the House unless he gave the undertaking required. —The motion was then put, and agreed to without a division. Mn. DlLLoet's ARREST. —Mr. PARNELL asked for the words or acts for which Mr. Dillon bad been arrested, and upon Mr. Forster declining to give any information beyond that contained in the warrant the hon. member for Cork pro- ceeded to denounce the Government for seeking to "evade a fair enquiry." He declared that his hon. friend suffered from an illness which required constant occupation in the open air to keep him alive, and that his imprisonment if it were long continued would result in his death or in his being crippled for life.—The PREMIER replied that it was the deliberate judgment of Parliament that the particulars asked for should not be given. If the hon. member for Cork I was prepared to make a charge against the Executive I Government, the Government would be prepared to meet it. —Mr. Forts= challenged Mr. Parnell to bring the matter forward by means of a motion impugning the conduct of the Government.—Mr. Cowen, Sir William Harcourt, Mr., Gibson, the Attorney-General for Irelacd, and Mr. Jesse Collings took part in the discussion.—Ueon the Speaker put- ting the question that the House do now adjourn, no mem- ber challenged his decision that the "Ayes" have it, and the House, therefore, stood adjourned shortly before nine o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. MR. BRADLATOR'S PROTEST.—The Speaker read a letter from Mr. Bradlaugh solemnly protesting in the name of the electors of Northampton against his expulsion from the House. In reply to Sir Wilfred Lawson, the SPEAKER said that the letter wouldappeatein the Votes, and it would be com- petent for any member to give notice that it might on a future day be brought under discussion, in which case it might be brought forward as a question of privilege. LAW op Liner..—Mr. HuTcunzsox moved the second reading of the Newspaper (Law of Libel) Bill. The objects of the Bill are to make privileged the reports of public meetings lawfully held, to require the fiat of the Attorney. General as apreliminary to criminal action for libel, and to provide for the registration of the proprietors of newspapers. The Bill was received with universal favour, tempered by some intimations that when it reached committee amend- ments on points of detail might advantageously be intro- duced.—Amongst the speakers were Mr. Inderwick, Mr. Gregory, Mr. Joseph Cowee, Mr. Macliver, Mr. Warton, Mr. Dil k e, Mr. McCarthy, and Mr. Labouchere.—The ATTORNEY- GENERAL, on behalf of the Government, expressed a hope that the Bill would be read a second time, which was forth- with done without a division. CLERICAL DISABILITIES BILL—Sir G. Goner= moved the second reading of the Clerical Disabilities Act Repeal Bill, the objectof which is to abolish Horne Tooke's Act and remove the prohibition against clergymen entering Parlia- ment—Mr. BEREBFORD HOPE, as a Ch Lachman, a CM istian, and a citizen, opposed the Bill, protesting against the intro- duction into Parliament of that most pestilent specimen of citizenship—the political parson. The Bill was opposed by Colonel Making, Sir John Mowbray, Mr. Warton, Mr. T. D. Sullivan, and Mr. Leighton. It was supported by Mr. H. Palmer, Mr. Hibbert, Mr. Gregory, and Sir W. Harcourt, who explained that unless the Bill included a declaratory clause that clergymen were entitled to sit in the House it would only bring back the difficulties that existed at the time of the passing of Horne Tooke's Act.—After some further discussion the Bill was rejected by 110 votes against 101—a result received with cheers and counter cheers. SMALL DEBTS BILL.—Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL moved the second reading of a Bill designed to limit the period for bringing actions for the recovery of small debts. After some conversation, in the course of which Sir Richard Cross advised him not to proceed further with the measure, he consented to withdraw the Bill. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY.

- - STOLEN GOODS BILL..—The LORD-CHANCELLOR moved the second reading of the Stolen Goods Bill, the object of which is to increase the powers of the police in dealing with the receivers of stolen property. He explained that pawn- brokers had been unnecessarily alarmed by an erroneous interpretation of the Bill, and said that it should be referred to a Select Committee, in order that evidence might be given by persons who considered themselves aggrieved.—The Marquis of SALISBURY criticised the Bill unfavourably, but offered no opposition, on the understandine that the ineisuro would be dealt with by a corn nittee.—The Bill was read a second time. CHARITABLE TRUSTS ACTS AMENDMENT Hil.L.—Vie LORD-CIIANCELLOR moved the second reading of Charitable Trusts Acts Amendment Bill, and explained that its object was to increase the powers of the Charity Commissioners in dealing with charitable trusts.—The Marquis of SALISBURY said that Bill would introduce an enormous change in the position of the Chat ity Commission towards every charitable trust in the country.—The Bill was read a second time. _ Intsrt LAND BILL, 1870.-1 return asked for by Earl Claim's, in reference to the two Land Bills of Mr. Gladstone was granted.

FRlDAT.—Before Messrs. W. Pilkington and E. Johnson (Es- Mayor. SAVAGE ASSAULT AT PEASLEY CROSS.—John Aspinall, James Aspinall, and Thomas Farrell, were each charged 1 with assaulting and beating George Green, on the 2nd May, at Peasley Cross.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, who appeared for the complainant, said Green was a horsekeeper, employed at Peasley Cross, nada- the Corporation, and the three defend- ants were employed as barrow men ur.der the Corporatisn. Green had control of the yard, and on Saturday it appeared I James Aspinall went to the yard and made a disturbance with a man named Bolton. Green went into the saddle- room to quell the disturbance, whereupon Aspinall threat- ened and struck him. Green then put him out of the yard, and there was an end of the matter for that day. On Mon- day, James Aspinall saw two women whom he told that "they had no malice against Mrs. Green, but there were four men who intended giving Green a good hiding." The three defendants arrive later in tie day and committed a most violent assault upon the complainant. They endeav- oured to pull out his eyes, also his tongue, knocked one of his teeth ont, and loosened others.—Complainant corrobor- ated this statement.—A Mrs. Smith said James Aspinall met her and another woman in the street on Monday, and at his request they went into a public-house and had some her. He there told them that they had no malice against Mrs. Green, but they intended giving Green a good hiding. He also said they need not tell Mrs. Green of the intended assault. She afterwards saw the complainant and the de- fendants struggling in Mrs. Holme's house, John Aspinall threw witnees down and kicked her, and be also struck I Father Byrne and tore his garments.—The defence was that Green dealt the first blow.—Mr. H. L. Riley appeared on behalf of the two Aspinalla—The magistrates fined John Aspioall and James Aspinall £3 each and costs, and Farrell £2 and costs, part of which fines will be appropriated towards the complainant's expenses.—Defendants applied for time to pay, but this was objected to by Mr. Swift on the ground that it would take away the sting of the punish- ment if granted.—Mr. Pilkington said it would prolong the punishment, and time was allowed. MoNnaT.—Before Mr. W. W. Pilkington and Mr. Willis. WORKING A HORSK IN AN UNFIT STATE.—WiIIi3M Littler, of Windle, was charged with working a horse whilst suffering from sores, and John Littler was summoned for causing the same to be worked on Friday afternoon.—P.O. Ratcliffe saw the horse drawing a harrow in John Littler's field, near Moss Bank railway station; and on examining it he found a sore four inches long, and three inches broad on its hip, part of which was scabbed over and cracked, the other part being quite raw. On touching its hip the horse screamed and kicked. He found another wound on the left shoulder.—John Littler said the horse did.not belong to him but to Mrs. Young.—The defendants were each fined 10s. and costs. STEALING IRON.—Charles Lawrenson, Eccleston was charged with having, en or about the 28th April, stoles an iron bolt worth 2g., the property of Frederick Outwaite.— Prosecutor said he was an enzie-0-. and resided at the IStanley Arms, Ecclestou. Ou iii.. 12th of April he was I employed by Mr. Edward Ratcliffe to take down some ; machinery at Windle Colliery, and that gentleman said pro- I secutor could have all the iron that was left, as it would not 'be worth the troublep get it out. The bolt produced was secreted with others, and Lawrenson went with him to put them away on the 27th. Lawrenson asked for a bolt, but prosecutor refused to give him one, as he was paid for his work. On the following day, the 28th April, he missed four bolts, and spoke to prisoner about the matter on the morning of the 29th. Prisoner denied having seen the bolts since their removal to the place of secresy. Re went with I the officer to the house of the prisoner, where they found the bolt produced.—P.C. George Young, stationed at Denton's-green,said on the 4th May he received the ; prisoner into custody from last witness. He charged him ; with stealing the bolt, when he replied, "1 did not steal it ; Oatwaite gave it to vne."—Prisoner said Outwaite gave him the bolt.—Richard Garnett said three bolts had been left on his premises by someone, but he did not know whom. Mr. Radley had promised to give him some bolts for sharpening some tools, but it appeared that he had made the same promise to Outwaite.—Prisoner was fined £2 and costs. ASSAULTING THE POLICE. Patrick Redmond was charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting on the 2nd May; and lie also, with William Rmain, was charged with assaulting the police.—P.C. Fielding said that about a quarter past eleven on Saturday night, Redmond was fighting with another man in Peter-street. He appre- hended him, and on getting into Liverpool-road at the corner of Arthur-street, on the way to the Town Hall, the prisoner said he would not go any further, and thereupon *truck the officer, and kicked him on the legs; from the effects of which kick he had been off duty since. Whilst struggling with the prisoner, Ruain came up and kicked him.—P.C. Smith corroborated the statement.—The prisoner Ruain said the officer was mistaken in the man who kicked him, as he ems asleep in the house at eleven o'clock at night.—Two policemen said they saw the prisoner in Ton- tine-street at ten minutes past eleven—five minutes before the time of the aSSanit.—Redmond was fined lOa. and costa, and bound over to keep the peace, and Ruain was fined £1 and costs for the assault.

div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
lIEALTII COMMITrEE.

The mont'ily meeting of this Committee was held el Wednesday, Dr. Twyford presiding. There were also pre- sent :—Alderman Mcßryde; Councillors Belsher, McKeeh- nie, Brook, Foster, Wilcock, Allen, with Dr. McNicell (medical officer), Mr. Hart (borough engineer), and Mr. Craik (deputy town clerk). TRH INFECTIODS DISEASES lIOSPITAL. The DEPUTY Toww CLERK said he had received a letter from the Local Government Board, and with it some sugges- tions respecting the Infectious Disoases Hospital at Peasley Vale. The suggestions were: Ist. That a trap should be inserted in the course of the main chain near to the tank, and an inlet for ventilation should be provided immediately on the house side of it. 2nd. The sewerage mud, liable, as it might be, to have infectious properties, should not be carted away, hut should be dug in at once on some of the spare land which the Town Council have acquired. 3rd. If practicable, it would be advisable that the effluent from the tanks sbottld not pass directly into the brook, but into a porous drain laid parallel vrlth it and at a few feet distant, so that the effluent may be filtered by passage through the earth. 4th. The straightening of the course of the brook is an improvement, but the removal of the obstruction at the culvert in the road should not be lost sight of. It was agreed to recornmend to the Connell the carrying out of the suggeatiime of the Local G3vernment Board.

TRE HORSE DRIVERS. The MAYOR congratulated the committee OR the good condition e* the Corporation horses. The condition of the horses Was'splendid on the May day's show, and he would suggest that each driver be presented with one day's pay as an encouragement to him to keep his horse in good condi- tion. The Liverpool Corporation used to give a dinner, but they had now done away with that, and each man received one day's pay. Ile hoped the committee would see their way to do likewise. The surveyor and other gentlemen who saw the horses would bear him out in what he had said. There were nine drivers. Ile would move that thev lee allowed one day's pay.

Gazette, and the Way in which he has reclaimed that famous journal under powerful opposition, so that it is now more generally popular, and more esteemed than it' ever was before, speaks much for the sagacity and enterprise of Mr. Thomp- son. The excellent speech which he delivered to the electors of Preston on Thursday night, win- ning over a large audience and exciting much en- thusiasm, is a sufficient indication that Mr. Thomp- son is an able exponent of Liberal principles, and We trust that he will have the warm and hearty support of the whole of the Liberal party in the borough. He comes befora the electors with unexceptionable credentials, and OA one who has an intimate knowledge of Irish affairs since he passed two or three years there as private secretary to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland at Dublin. During his residence there, at a very important period—the time when the Irish Land Bill of 1870 was being discussed and put into shape--he obtained much valuable informatiom from all classes with regard to the nature of the wants of the land popula- tion, so that he would be a valuabk member of the present House of Commons. We were pleased to notice the fearlessness with whit& Mr. Thompson gave expression to his independent opiuion of the policy ot the Liberal Government with regard to Irish affairs, when he said that, although he had in the main all his life agreed with the policy of Mr. Glad- stone, he,differed from him on the one question of a eoercive policy, showing that with him it will be an advocacy of principles and not of persons.. Seeing then that Mr. Thompson is a true Liberal, a szentle- man thoroughly conversant with the staple industries of this county, one who ie connected with various public bodies which have a high opinion of his administrative ability and general ussfulness, and a Lancashire .man, we shall watch with keen interest the contest at Preston, and heartily wish that he may be successful in destroying the Tory monopoly of the representation of that borough.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

At the last meetisg of the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners, Mr. Frith drew attention to a subject of considerable interest to the town. It appears that several pices of land belonging to Runcorn freeholders have been taken posses- sion of bY various people living in the neighbourhood, apparently in the firm belief that there is no little modicum of truth in the old'saying that possession is nine points of the law. One of the speakers alleged that a certain limb of the law, in the perron of a lawyer's clerk, had taken this course, and when appealed to upon the subject he very cavalierly declined even to answer the letter which had been sent to him. Perhaps he believes in another old saying, which is certainly rather commonplace, but is usually rendered in the vernacular as " The least's said, the soonest mended." It is a valuable acquisition to be able to keep one's tongue still on certain occasions. Our much abused friend Thomas Carlyle, said that silence was golden whilst speech was only silvern; and if he could only obtain per- mission to visit " these glimpses of the moon" and see what the reviewers are saying about him, and his unfortu- nate production now being published as his " Reminis- censes, ' he would probably be of opinion that he had not sufficiently followed out Iris own teaching, but had given too much rein to a carping, critical spirit that is likely to materially injure his former fair fame. Several of the Com- missioners expressed themselds in no measured terms as to the conduct of the people who had thus taken upon them- selves to tamper with the inalienable rights of the free- holders, and expressed an opinion to the effect that immediate action ought to be initiated to put a stop to such proceed- kw's. A oommittge was appointed to investigate the matter.

One would have imagined that there had been lively scenes sufficient to satisfy any one with reasonable requirements at the meetings of commissioners held during the last six months, but I perceive that my energetic friend, Dr. McDougall was again to the front. This time he seems to have taken the surveyor to task on the ground that he was not a geologist, or as well up in the various strata as Hugh Miller, the speaker's fellow countryman. I, however, fail to see much judgment in the deduction drawn by Dr. McDougall from the fact that Mr. Barker was not a geologist, which was apparently, that because of the lamentable deficiency in his education, he was no better able to judge of the quality of stone than any individual member of the Board It is hardly to be supposed that Mr. Barker has not gained a certain amount of valuable knowledge as to stone during the many years he has had to do with it, and tinder these circumstances, I must, with much regret, say that I think Dr. McDougall did not display the usual gOO4 judgment which is so marked a feature of his -speeches. The chairman Mr. George Marshall) during the course of the discussion, save the doctor a pretty hard rap upon the knuckles to the effect that be was always making explanations on some subject or more I censured aonpdporhteunalitsyo of tf r ospeaking toht ha enr 0, ni neeo rudpeor nt oa oqbuteasi tilionan; the speaker for daring to say that he (the chairman) was being made a cat's-paw by Mr. Robert Shaw.

Catherine Marshall, the young Scotch damsel, whose strong aversion to food is exciting some sensation, is not after all to be alicwed to share the fate of her prototype Miss Jacobs, the Welsh fasting girl. Catherine has been very plainly told that if she does not eat she will be -sent to a lunatic asylum. The effect has been magical, for the young lady soon found her appetite, and the last report states that She was taking food. What a pity somehody did not think of it earlier. If the same fate was threatened to people who believe in such nonsensical stories it would soon put an end to the fasting mania.

I have seen a pleasing innovation upon the China paint- ing which has been so much affected by ladies recently. The new artistic recreation is shell painting. By skilful fingers the unpreposeeeeittg oyster shell is transformed into a miniature laMiscape or sea view in oils. For winter scenes the bright whiteness of the inner side of the shell is beAuti- fully adapted, and I have seen 801110 very pretty efforts of art prepared la this manner. A curious superstition still finds currency among many horticultural inhabitants in the surrounding districts. An old man informed me the other day that the 7th of May was for some occult reason specially adapted for the plantiug.of French beans. lie is himself a firm believer in the tradi- tion, and informed me that that day was regarded as one of unusual good omen by a very large number of gardeners in the neighbourhood.

Judging from a paragraph in your columns on Saturday last, the Toronto Telegram appears to think that there ie great future before the port of Runcorn, consequent upon an expected change in the location for manufacturing salt in the county of Chester. I suppose that the writer bases his remark upon the formation of the Mersey Brine Scheme Company, to which every Ituncornian wishes success.

The people of Widnes are quite jubilant about the large increase which the recent census shows the town to have made during the last decade, the population now stand- ing, in round numbers, at 25,000. A cloud now hangs over the commercial affairs of the town, which it is hoped will soon disperse. FLAtCUS.

Last. the men employed by the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, agreed to contract themselves out of the Employers' Liability Act, and during the month the firm have handed the handsome sum of £72 to the widowof William Manning, the poor Sallow:sato was drowned ill -a cesspool at their manufactory. Mn. C. Bnutwan's Oran,. COAXIt RuNconw. Saturday evening, this company gave their second performance in the Public Hall, Runcorn, to a large house. I Miss Alexina Andersen, as Servo/me, took the part to per- fection, her vivacity and finished acting frequently drawing I forth the hearty applause of the audience. Mr. JasCtm- herland, as the Bailee, was irresistible ; and Mr. Danvers, as Goo, kept the spectators in nearly a constant roar of laugh- ter from the beginning to the end of the piece. The part of Gaepard, the old miser, was remarkably well played by Mr. T. li. York. Miss Clara Harrington, as Germaine, was, if anything, a little too hoydeNish and wanting in self-posses- sion for the part, though her manner was ladylike. The entire company gave general satisfaction, and it is, pro- ') ihly, one of the strongest which Mr. Bernard has travel- ling. We n,ust net conclude our Somewhat brief notice without a dof praise to Mr. J. C. Moreton, the accorn- PlWbed and gentlemanly agent of the company, whose courtegy was the subject of general remark.

RUNCORN PRIMITIVE METRODISM.—TIII4 Rev. Joseph Morton, now of Runcorn, has been sele,ctta by the district meeting at Fleetwood, as the minister, to the Warrington and Widnes station.

-- SUCCESS OF li. WIDNES AT' .... Mr. J. Concan- non, of Widnes, carried off ~,. second prize in the One Mile Steeplechase Handicap, ao. Birmingham, on Saturday. Mr. Snook, Moseley Haul.'" took 6rst place. Time, 5 min. r 25 sec.

SERUONS AT ST. MIGHLEL'I3, bITTON.—On Sunday, the Rev. Francis James Henry, S.J., preached two sermons e St. Michael's Catholic Church, Ditton, in aid of St. Mary's schools. There were large congregations. High Mass, by Rampis, was celebrated in the morning, and the musical part of the service was ably rendered by the German choir of the church.

SIMMONS AT WIDNES.—The Rev. J. Graham, of Birkenhead, preached two sermons in connection with Simms' Cross Primitive Methodist Sunday School, on Sun- day. A children's service was also held in the afternoon, when Mr. S. Davies, of Manchester, occupied the chair. The collections amounted to upwards of £7.

PRIXIITVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.— The annual sermons on behalf of this school were preached on Sunday, in the Greenway-road chapel, by the Rev. Wm. Rowe, ex-president of the Conference. In the afternoon, a service of song, entitled "Home, sweet home," was given by the children. The readings were by the Rev. J. Bate- man (Wesleyan Methodist), who undertook the duty in the unavoidable absence of Mr. Thomas Norman, through a slight indisposition. The collections realised upwards of £24.

RUNCORN CAMDEN BAND HOPE.—On Monday evening a public meeting was held in connection with this society. Mr. T. Norman presided. Mr. S. C. Beckett gave an appropriate address, which was listened to with very great attention. Miss Kirkham rendered a recitation called "The wife's resolve" in a very beautiful manner. Mr. J. Williams gave another on "The address to the bottle," which was rendered in a very masterly style. A dialogue concerning " Miss Burton's troubles with her domestics " followed, and all who took Dart in it deserved praise for the manner in which they went through their respective parts.—Gene. GREAT SANZEY ANNIVERSARY SERVICRS.—The an- niversary services in connection with the Great Sankey Day and Sunday Schools were held on Sunday last. In the morning, the Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar of Widnes, took part in the service ; and the afternoon service was conducted by the Rev. T. Louch, Warrington, who gave an earnest address to scholars, teachers, and friends. The evening service was conducted by the Rev. T. Chambers, of Halewood. The congregations were very large, and the col- lections realised about £2O. The esteemed vicar of Great Sankey, the Rev. E. S. Jackson, took part in the services for the first time after his late illness. Suitable hymns were sung in a very creditable manner by the choir and children; Miss Standish presiding with her usual ability at the organ.

THE SAD DEATH OF I RUNCORN MAN AT LEIGH.— On Monday, at the Leigh Petty Sessions, John Whittle, canal boatman, surrendered to his bail on the charge of unlawfully causing the death of Thomas Nichols, canal boatman, of Runcorn, on the 30th ult.—Superintendent Jackson stated that the two men quarrelled in a publie-house, outside which they went to fight, the result being that Nichols was killed) The facts have been fully reported in The Examiner. The Superintendent asked that, as sufficient evidence could not be obtained to warrant a committal to the assizes for manslaughter, the accused should be discharged.—Mr. Johnson remarked that the quarrel took place in a public- house, and he hoped the sad end of it would be a caution to him against drinking.—Prisoner was then discharged. PRESENTATION AT RIINCOUN.-011 the evening of the sth inst., the teachers of the NeW/OWD Mission Sunday Schoo/, Runcorn, met at the Schoolroom, Shaw-street, and having partaken of tea provided by the superintendent, the Rev. Canon Barclay was voted to the chair. Mr. Pownall gavel a short address on the earnestness required in Sunday school work, and afterwards presented Miss Cropper with a hand- somely bound illustrated Bible, subscribed for by the teachers, as a token of their esteem and good wishes on her approaching marriage. Mr. Cropper responded. The Bible contained the following inscription, neatly written by Mr. J. B. Imison, of Widnes:—" To Miss Cropper, from the teachers of the Newtown Mission Sunday School, as a token of their esteem. May sth, 1881." During the eveningsongs were sung by Messrs. R. Wainwright, E. Key, and C. and I. Pownall. Mr. Roberts also gave a reading, and Mr. C. Pownall a harmonium solo. A Ruuconti TRADESMAN'S PUREE/AL.—The mortal re- mains of Mr. Samuel Briscoe, of Bridgewater-street, Run- corn, the son of Mr. Peter Briscoe, were interred at the cemetery on Monday last. A very fair number of the mem- bers of the Oddfellows' lodge with which deceased was con- nected, joined he the procession, Amongst deceased's fel- low tradesmen who attended were Mr. G. Marshall, Mr. C Houghton- and Mr. J. Timperley. In the first coach were the Rev. Canon Barclay and Dr. Carruthers. The bearers were Mr. John Briscoe, Mr. Samuel Crosby, Mr. Thomas Lydiate, and Mr. Samuel Blair. Masters James and Peter Briscoe, sons of the deceased, with Mr. Peter Briscoe, Mr. James Price, Mr. Henry Briscoe. and Mr. John Price oc- cupied the -second coach. In the third were Mr. Samuel. Crosby, Mr. Joseph Booth, Mr. Thomas Price, Mr. John Ball, and Mr. E. Gregory. The service in the church an. at the grave side was conducted by the Rev. Canon Barclay. A large number of persons assembled at the cemetery to wit- ness the interment.

Wrosrgs Parma entrEat SCROOL.9.—The fourteenth and last of these entertainments, was given on Tuesday evening. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar, who, during the course of the evening, said that the nett money result of the various entertainments had been the raising of £25 towards the class-room fund, and £5 towards the purchase of a piano. To the former there nod& haveto be added the receipts that night. The follow- ing programme was afterwards gone through :—Glee, "Ohl who will o'er the downs so free, Glee class; Sang, "Then you'll remember me," Miss Fairley ; Solo Piccolo, " The Pirate of Penzance," Mr. S. SPECILL'CIIIIIRCH SERVICES AT 013.1•011D.—Sermori8 in aid of the Orford Church schools were preached at Orford, on Sunday, that in the morning by the Rev Canon Sharp, M.A., vicar of •Swavesey, and in the evening by the Rev. Morley Stevenson, M.A., clerical principal of the Clergy Daughters' schools. The collections for the day amounted to .513 ss.

THE POLICE lUND THE WEST CHESHIRE ELECTIO2C—The following general order has been issued by Captain Arrow- smith, chief constable of the county, In reference to the recent election in West Cheshire :—General Order. Chief Constable's Office,Chester, May sth, 1881.—It is a source of much gratification to the Chief Constable to be able to congratutate the force on the excellent temper and disci- pline displayed by it under, in some cases, very trying ,•circumstances, during the late parliamentary election for ,West Cheshire. This was made more especially prominent at Nantwich on the 22nd ult., where, but for the forbearance I of the constabulary and the efficient manner in which they I were commanded by Superintendent Mayo and Captain Liugard, a serious disturbance might have taken place. such conduct nedounds to the credit of the whole force, in- creases public confidence in it, and in this instance has called forth the commendation at the magistrates at Nant- wick in petty sessions assembled. The foregoing order will be read at the head of divisions by superintendents at their seat weekly parade.

MERSEY SALT AND BRINE COMPANY LIMITED.—We are informed teat the lettem of allotment of the Mersey Salt and Brine Company Limited,were posted last night, Friday, and that the works gre to be commenced forthwith. TEE POPULATION or LANCASIIIRE.—The population of Lancashire, according to the census returns just completed, is close upon three and a half millions—an increase since the last census of nearly 650,000, or at the rate of about 20 per cent.

CHILD SCALDED TO DEATH AT RUNCORN.—On Thurs- day, an inquest was held at the Navigation Inn, Canal- street, Runcorn, by Mr. Worsley, deputy-coroner, on the body of Jacob Bradbury, aged one year and four montbs,the son of John Bradbury, Wivern-place. On the previous Sunday, whilst Mrs. Bradbury was cooking dinner, she put a cup full ot hot water on the table, which the little one knocked over, and scalded itself severely. A doctor was sent for, and the usual remedies applied, but the child died on the following day.. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

Mr. Justice Matthew, in charging the grand jury at Liverpobl assizes, on Monday, referred to the necessity of an alteration in the criminal law, and said he could not see why it should not be allowed to a convicted prisoner in this country, as it was in every other country, to appeal against a sentence which be thought too severe. THE COLLIERS OF EARLESTOWN.—On Wednesday even- ing, a mass meeting of colliers was held upon the Market Ground, Earlestown, to consider the reductions that are made in their wages for picksharpening, Sze., also other grievances. Mr. Cross, of St. Helens, presided. They de- termined to resist all encroachments upon their wages, and not rest satisfied until they got an advance. THE CANIBRIDGE LOCAL EXAMINATION.---ThC report of the Syndicate on the Cambridge Local Examination held in December, 1880, has just been published. We understand that the Sizarship, together with £3O per annum for two years, which is offered annually by St. John's College to the best senior candidate in the Cambridge Local Examinations, who shall have obtained the mark of distinction both in Latin and in Greek, has been awarded this year to W. W. Reiland, of the Lancaster Royal Grammar School.

THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR WEST CHESHIRE.—Mr. James Tomkinson, the Liberal candidate at the late election for West Cheshire, attended a meeting of the executive com- mittee of the Birkenhead district, at the Liberal Club, Hamilton-square, Birkenhead, on Wednesday, and made ar- rangements with them respecting the registration of vot3rs, and other matters connected with the division; after which he was entertained to dinner at the Club by Mr. George Atkin, the chairman of Birkenhead Liberal Association. There was a numerous party of invited guests. LANCASHIRE COTTON SPINNERS AND THE FRENCH TARIFF.—At a meeting of the central committee of the North and North-East Lancashire Cotton Spinners and Manufacturers' Association, at the Mitre Hotel, Manches- ter, on Tuesday, the question of the new French tariff came under consideration, and the following resolution (a copy of which the secretary was directed to forward to the Govern- ment) was passed :—" That this association urges the Government not to accept any new treaty with France of a less favourable character to the cotton spinning and manu- facturing interests of this country than „the treaty now expiring.

. _ *TEMPERANCE ENTERTAINMENT LT THELWILL. —ln connection with the Grappenhall and Thelwall Total Ab- stinence Society, an entertainment was held in the Tem- perance Hall, Thelwall, on Monday evening. There was a large audience, and Mr. R. A. Naylor, of Cuerdon Hall, occupied the chair. Songs were given by the Misses Bed- dard and Waterfield (Warrington), /11i9ii Daintik (Widnes), and Mr. S. Shakeshaft (Grappenhall); and duets by Mr. Griffiths and Miss Wood (Warrington.) Mr. J. Cottam per- formed a solo on the dulcimer, and Mr. Bosteck (Warring- ton) ,a pianoforte solo, which werewell received. A reading in the Lancashire dialect by Mr. Harding (Thelavall), caused much amusement. In the course of the evening an address was delivered by Mr. C. Plinston (Warrington), on tem- perance. A pleasant evening was brought to a close by the usual votes of thanks.

The following are the 54 members who voted in the minority in favour of the previous question on the proposal of the Prime Minister to erect a national monument to the late Earl of Beaconsaeld:—Messrs. Anderson, J. S. Balfour, Barclay, Barran, Beaumont, Biggar, Briggs, Jacob Bright, Burt, Bryne, Caine, Charles Cameron, Jesse Collings, W. J. Corbet, Dawson, Baron de Ferrieres, Dillwyn, the Hon. W. Egerton, Finigan, Sir A. Gordon, Healy, F. Henderson, Hop. ' wood, Illingworth, Sir W. Lawson, Laycock, Leahy, Lee, M‘Donald, Justin M‘Carthy, J. G. McMinnies, Mappin, Mason, Isaac Nelson, T. P. O'Connor, 1). M. O'Connor, Peddie, Pennington, Philips, Potter, Rylands, B. Samuelson, Slagg. T. E. Smith, P. A. Taylor, the lion. L. Stanley, Thomarson, Webster, Whitworth, S. C. MR. liial.nrivras, ALP., d.T LEYIAND,--A four days' bazaar was opened at Leyland, near Preston. on Wednesday, by Mr. 3. G. McMinnies, M.P.. for Warrington, in aid of the liquidation of the debt on the Congregational church and school in that township. The buildings were erected at a cost of £4,500, towards which Mr. McMinnies has contri- buted about £1,200, including the site, and now by the bazaar it is expected that a sum of about £650 will be raised, which will clear off the rem)ining debt. In the course of his observations, Mr. McMinuies said he would wish to see a more united Christian spirit prevail in the land, so that people might regard each other ,"ore as brothers than monsters when they happened to differ in religious opinions. Respecting bazaars, he said some folks strongly objected to them; he, for one, did not. (Hear, bear.) In a speech which he read recently, he found that a very eminent man of that part of the county spoke very disparagingly and very disrespectfully of bazaars, and especially did he seem to have an antipathy for antimacassars, for they were always sticking to men's buttons. (Laughter.) Well, at bazaars, there were many useful and ornamental things, and antima- cassars were certainly aeuseful as the two buttons behind the Bishop of Manchester's coat, to which the antimacassar^ ap- peared to stick. (Laughter and applause.)

ASSOCIATION OP INSPECTORS OF WEIGHTS AND MEASURES.—The inaugural meeting of the British Associa- tion of Inspectors of Weights and Measures was commenced on Monday, in the Mayor's Parlour at the Town Hall, Man- chester. Mr. W. S. Brown, chairman of the Weights and Measures Committee of the Manchester Corporation, pre- sided. At the afternoon's sitting Mr. T. Wimhurst read a paper entbled, "My experiences of the Weights and Measures Acta." The officers of the Association were after- wards elected, Mr. W. S. Brown (Manchester) being ap- pointed president, Mr. Alderman Chandley (Warrington) vice-president, Mr. Hopkins (Manchester) treasurer, Mr. Wimhurst (Manchester) secretary, and Messrs. Robinson (Stockport), Johnson (Salford), Place (Warrington), Grime (Wigan), Gregory (Birkenhead), and Parkin (Sheffield), as members of the committee for the ensuing twelve months. The members of the Association dined together in the even- ing at the Albion Hotel, Piccadilly. The Mayor of Man- chester (Mr. Alderman Baker) occupied the chair, and the Mayor of Salford (Mr. Alderman Robinson) the vice-chair. After the usual loyal and patriotic toasts, the Chairman pro- posed the toast of the evening—" Success to the British I Association of Inspectors of Weights and Measures." He said that they were met for the purpose of remedying a very defective Act of Parliament. If the Act of MS had been drawn with the care and attention which so important a subject +demanded, there would have been no necessity for inspectors of weights and measures becoming associated to- gether. Some time would elapse before any substantial alteration could be made in it, but he believedif they sought to increase the influence of their Association they would, after some years, obtain an amended Act. (Applause.)—Mr. E. Place (Warrington) briefly responded.--Mr. Alderman Chandley gave "The Mayors of Manchester and Salford." —Mr. Wimhurst afterwards proposed "The Visitors," to which Mr. Parnell responded.—Other toasts followed.

THE SOUTHPORT AND LANCASHIRE BANKING COAL- PAN; LIMITED.—The petitioners of Mr. T. M. Wilkinson, and another and of Messrs. Chadwick and Co. for winding up the company came on for hearing before the Master of the Rolls on Saturday.—Mr. Chitty, Q.C., who appeared upon one of the petitions, stated that there had been a reso- lution of the shareholders to wind up voluntarily, and the petition stood over from time to time to give an opportunity for the reconstruction of the company. That scheme though not quite complete, was carried out, and a very large number of the new shares were already subscribed for, and it was expected that the whole of the preference shares were already subscribed for. At present, however, this was not done, but the scheme would be carried into effect. It was now proposed theta supervision order should be taken, with instructions to the liquidator founded on the resolution of the shareholders at a meeting held on the 11th of March. The shares were £330,000 and £220,000, for which share- holders to nearly the whole amount had come in under tilt new scheme. If his Lordship could give some intimation to the liquidator, either by the present order or by summons, so that they might go on, that it would be beneficial to all parties, he would take the order in that form.—Mr. Ince, Q.C., and Mr. Roxburgh, Q.C., maid they consented to this course.—Mr. Chitty said the provisional agreement that had been entered into provided that what was to be done should be done with the emotion of the court.—The Master of the Rolls? Then you do not want anything from the court?— Mr. Ince, Q.C., said he appeared for the liquidator as well for the company, and he consented.—Mr. Chitty said the liquidators were authorised to sell to a new company that had been got up.—The Master of the Rolls observed that ` that had nothing to do with the Aupervision ordm—Mr. Chitty said a resolution was come to by the shareholders at a meeting, and it was provided that what was to be done should be done with the sanction of the court.—The Master of the Rolli said he did not see any occasion for a super- vision order. However, as it was asked for by all parties. they had a right to have it.—Mr. Chitty; -We will provide fir the cost:L-11e Master of the Rolls: I am sure I should be very anzioas to do without a winding up.—His Lordship then made one order for winding up the company under supervision ef the court on both petitions, with the usual order as to costs.

LOCAL PROPERTY SALE AT Sr. HELENS. —On Thursday evening, May 12, the undermentioned lots of free- hold property were offered for sale by public auction, by Mr. Birchall, at the Fleece Hotel, St. Helens. Lot 1. A freehold dwelling-house, No. 40, Albert-street ; the bidding commenced at £5O, which rapidly increased to £126, at ' which sum the lot was sold. Lot 2. A freehold dwelling- house, No. 187, college-street; the bidding commenced at £lOO, and was sold at £230. Lot 3. A freehold butcher's shop and dwelling-house adjoining, 123 and 125, College- street, were sold for£4ss. Mr. Brcwis was the solicitor for the vendor. PRESCOT WESLEYAN Crterm..—Ort Sunday last, two sermons were preached, morning and evening, in the above place of worship, by the Rev. J. A. B. Harry, superintendent minister of the circuit. There was a Very gold attendance at both services, and the collections realised the sum of £9 10s. On Monday evening a special service was held in the chapel, at which the sermon was preached by the Rev. T. T. Lambert, of Liverpool. Special hymns were sung in a creditable manner by the children attending the Sunday schools. There was only a small congregation, not nearly so large as last year. The collection amounted to about £3. The proceeds of Sunday and Monday are to be devoted to the school funds.

INDEPENDENT SUNDAY SCHOOLS, ST. HELENS.—The 75th anniversary of the Sunday schools in connection with the Congregational church, was celebrated on Sunday, when the Rev. J. W. Walker, of Huyton, preached in the morning, and addressed the scholars in the afternoon ; and the Rev. Hugh Stowell Brown, of Liverpool, preached in the evening. The evening attendance was very large, but the morning service was only fairly attended. Special hymns were sung in the afternoon. The amount collected last year proved in- sufficient to cover the expenses of the year, and an appeal was made to the congregation for a special effort to clear off the debt of last year, and provide for the expenses of the current one. £6O was the sum stated as required; but the collections realised .£47 10s.

A PDESCOT ROUGH AT MOSTYN.—Before the justices at Holywell, John Edward Thomas was charged with being drunk and assaulting the police. Sergeant Jones stated that he apprehended the prisoner at Mostyn, on Monday, under a warrant for drunkenness, when the prisoner became mo t violent, hit him on the head, endeavoured to trip him up, and kicked him repeatedly with heavy clogs. P.C. Adams, who went to the sergeant's assistance, was also kicked by the prisoner, who in his straggles got his foot into the officer's trousers pocket and tore it down. The prisoner was committed to Chester Castle for two months with bard labour for the assault, and to a further term of 14 days for drunkenness, in default of paying a tine and costs of 235. It was stated that prisoner had only just been released from prison, where he had been confined for three months for assaulting the police at Prescot. MR. HENRY WOOD'S PICTURE IN TICE ROYAL Acannwr.—ln a critique on the Royal Academy Exhibition the Saturday Review thus speaks of Mr. Henry Wood's pic- ture :—" At the Foot of the Rialto, Venice" (61), is ad- mirable. alike in composition, drawing, colour, and in the sense of picturesque life which pervades an attractive work. The Manchester Guardian says :—A little picture not to be passed over in this room is the view of the Rialto at Venice (61), by Mr. Henry Woods, very bright in colour, and with a successful impression of the moving life of the city street, but not wholly satisfactory in the manner of its execution. Mr. Woods is a young artist who has not acquired all the technical power that he needs for doing full justice to his intention. The excellence of the painting is in the inverse order of the importance of the facts represented. There is more mastery in the rendering of the cabbages in the fore- ground than is to be found in the faces or forms of the figures; there is more beauty in the diffused sunlight rest- ing upon the stall of fruit to the right of the composition than theartpilset has been able to bestow upon the crowd of m passing up and down the narrow street. But in spite of these defects the picture is in many respects an excellent and promising performance, which is to be clearly distinguished from a mass of vulgar genre painting which disfigures the exhibition. The Man:hester Courier observes: In the far corner of the north wall is a charming bit of Venice, exquisitely rendered by Mr. Henry Woods, who paints the market "At the foot of the Rialto" with a rare skill and truthfulness demanding a roach better position.

"GREAT HEART" LODGE (No. 2,363).— On Saturday evening last, the usual weekly entertainment under the auspices of the above lodge, and aided by a few friends, was given in Ackary's Cocoa Rooms, Shaw-street St. Helens. Brother Brockbank presided in a very efficient manner. The meeting was opened by the company joining in the sacred song, "Work for the night is coming," after which the chairman introduced a few appropriate remarks on the principles of temperance applied to Oa home, which was followed by a song "Merry Dick," given by Brother Kemp in capital style, and was loudly applauded. This was followed by a reading, "The Drunkard's Looking Glass," rendered by Brother Glover in a ~ery pleasing manner. Sister Mellor then gave one of her humourous songs, accompanied on the concertina, " Good Old Jeff," which was received with loud applause. A short paper on the "History of Temperance." was read by Brother Lawrenson, succeeded by a reading "Public House Signs," by Brother Bird, after which Sister Eccleston delighted the meeting by singing in a charming manner the sacred song "Scattered Seeds of Kindness," accompanied on the harmonium by Bro. Gorbutt. Brother Achary, ever willing to advance the cause of temperances gave a short address, after which Sisters Eccleston and Brown enlivened the meeting by A duet "Room among the Angels." After a song from Brother Got- butt," Never forget the dear ones," the meeting was addres- sed for a short time in a very earnest manner by Brother Guttridge, of Haydock. The song "Once again we meet," by Brotl er Lowe, was followed by an amusing reading en- titled" The confession," by Brother Cord. A recitation by Brother Jones, and a duet by the two juvenile sisters Miss L Ackerav, and Miss Amy Gorbutt, "Let our hearts be always cheerful," concluded the programme, the entertain- ment being brought to a close by the company singing the hymn "What a friend we have in Jesus."

ALLEGED NON-DELIVERY OF SALT BY THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.—At the St. Helens County'Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. T. P. E. Thomp- son, judge, the case of Messrs. Richard Evans & Co. v. the London and North-Western Railway Company and Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., Widnes, was heard. The claim was for LII for salt supplied.—Mr. Dismore of the firm of Thornely and Dismore, Liverpool) appeared for the plain- tiffs, Mr. Preston appeared for the company, and Mr. Carver, barrister (instructed by Messrs. 11. Forshaw and Hawkins, solicitors, Liverpool), represented Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co. —Mr. Dismore said the contents of three boats laden with salt were delivered at the Widnes Dock, on the 9th and 11th August last, to the London and North-Western Rail- way Company for delivery to Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., chemical manufacturers, Widnes. The salt was loaded on trucks, and whilst the company alleged that the whole of the waggons were delivered, Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co. denied the receipt of nine waggons, and refused to pay for them. Mr. Preston then proceeded to call evidence to show that the waggons in dispute were delivered. Mr. Carver's contention was that the waggons had not been received, as there was no entry in any of the books kept by Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, anl Co. to that effect, and notice of them would have been taken by three different ser- vants to the firm if they had arrived, but they had never been seen. Three witnesses, named Morris, Caldwell, and Brown, gave evidence for the defence, after which His Honour said he saw nothing whatever to throw discredit or doubt on the servants in the employ of the railway com- pany. He could not say he was quite satisfied with the way in which the evidence was given by some of the servants of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co. He did not say there was any intention to mislead, but it struck him that there was an appearance in the manner of the witnesses that they felt they were in some scrape or other, and that prevented them giving the proper answers to the questions, which men of ordinary intelligence would have understood. His Honour's suspicion was that the salt had gone into Gasket', Deacon, and Co.'s warehouses, where it was lost among the multi- tudinous tons of salt that were there at the time. He then gave judgment for the railway company with costs, and judgment for the plaintiffs as against Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co. The case occupied the court upwards of three hours.

SUPPOSED CONCEALMENT OF BIRTH AT APPLETON.— On Monday, an inquest was held at the Elephant and Angel Inn, Appleton, near Widnes, by Mr. Driffield, county coroner, on the body of a newly-born male child, which, on the 6th inst., was found at a few inches below the surface in St. Bede's Catholic burial ground.—James Brown, gardener and sexton at the burial ground, said that on Friday last, about half-past eleven in the morning, be noticed that the surface of a grave which had recently been decorated with flowers had been disturbed. On examination he found part of a dress protruding through the cart. Searching further, a few inches below the surface he found the body of a male child. He informed Drs. Cooper and Booth, who saw the body. and it was afterwards placed in a stable adjoining the 1 Elephant and Angel lon. He had not the slightest idea by I whom the body had been placed in the graveyard.—Dr. Cooper said on Friday he was told by Dr. Booth about the body being found. He and Dr. Booth accompanied by the grave digger, went to the room behind the priest's residence, where the body was lying. He found it was that of a male child, which had been dead three or four days. There were no external marks of violence upon it. On Saturday even- ing witness made a post-mortem examination of the both-. He found the lungs fairly dilated, which was proof that the child had breathed. The internal organs were bloodless, and in all probability death had been caused by hcemorrhage owing to neglect at the time of birth. There were no actual injuries or anything to suggest suffocation or other intentional cause of death. The child was fully developtd. —The Coroner, in summing up, said that it was satisfactory to know that the child had never really lived. It had evidently died very shortly afterbirth, as was proved by the doctor's evidence. He thought it satisfactory that there had been no violence. There had been neglect and conceal- ment, but there did not seem to have been anything more in the caee.—ln reply to Mr. Driffield, Inspector Barnett said the police had no information as to the parties who were concerned in the matter, nor had they any prospect of doing so at present.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the child had been born alive, but bad died from loketnorrbage, owing to want of attention immediately after birth. ,

NEW WRIT.—A new writ was issued for Preston. TM; HOLDING OF AssizEs.—Sir W. HARCOURT said the question of the number of assizes for trial of prisoners WU under consideration, with a view of seeing whether a mere convenient system than that which existed could ,be adopted.
MASSACRE OP CHINESE IN PERU-Sir C. DUKE said it was quite true that a massacre of Chinese had taken place in Peru, but steps had been taken to protect the English sub- jects there.

Tits Bops.—Mr. CHILDFRS said he had no reason to believe that the unprecedented number of English killed in proportion to wounded was not to be attributed to the use of explosive bullets by the Boers.

IRISH ARRESTS.—A discussion took place on the arrest of James Lalor, in Queen's County.—Mr. FonsTEn denied that the man had been arrested or that the county was pro- claimed to enable landlords to evict tenants and collect rents.

Mn. BRADLAUGH'S CASE.—Mr. LenouctrEnn, appealing to Sir W. Lawson, said the removal of the word "illegal" would make his resolution simply one to rescind resolution passed the 26th April. Carrying that resolution would not facilitate Mr. Bradlaugh taking his seat, and therefore he asked the Prime Minister what course he proposed to take with regard to the Parliamentary Oaths Bill. He, under all circumstances, asked Sir W. Lawson to withdraw his reso- lution. He moved that the House adjourn.—Sir W. LAW- SON, amid cheers and laughter, seconded. He said that having to move the reaolution without the word "illegal had made an alteration of his course necessary. He would not move his altered resolution without notice. He would, however, bring it forward some day, of which he would give ample notice, but he would net lying it forward Lowever at all if tactics to prevent the Attorney-General bringing I forward his bill to amen] the Parliamentary Oaths Act were given up.—Lord R. Cnnuctor.r, made observations to the effect that in all Mr. Bradlaugh had done he bad acted under the inspiration of the Prime Minister and others.— Mr. GrAnsrotrx rose and contended the noble lord was not in order in making such an assertion after the declaration he had naade the other day.— Lord R. CHURCHILL withdrew the offensive obser- vation, and asked whether Sir W. Lawson could deny that Mr. Bradlaugh so acted.—The SPEAKER ruled Lord Churchill out of order.—Lord CnoncErta, withdrew the offensive expression, and asked whether it was possible for Sir Wilfrid Lawson to hold his resolution over the House in terrorism.—Mr. GLADSTONE denied that Government was in concert either with Mr. Bradlaugh, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, or Mr. Labouchere. With respect to the Parliamentary Oath Bill it would be better to adjourn the further discussion of that Bill until after the Irish Land Bill was disposed of.—

div.head: SERVANT'S SCRUPLES.
div.p: A SERVANT'S SCRUPLES.

- At the Oldham County Court, yesterday, a domestic ser— vant named Lettice Jacobs, sued her mistress for wages under somewhat extraordinary circumstances. She stated that she left the house because of a corpse being there, and did not return for two nights, when she was not allowed to begin her work. His Honour slid a servant had no right to leave because a corpse was in a house, and a verdict must be given for the defendant.

div.head: CHESHIRE SALT DISTRICTS COMPENSATION BILL. (Continued front Page C.)
div.p: CHESHIRE SALT DISTRICTS COM- PENSATION BILL. (Continued front Page C.)

Sir Sidney Waterlow again presided at the sittirg of the committee on Friday. Mr. Maskell Peace. the secretary and law clerk to the Mining Association of Great Britain, secretary to the South Lancashire and Cheshire Coal As- sociation, and the Town Clerk of Wigan, said this Bill would interfere with what was understood to be the law, that in the working of mines colliery proprietors were at liberty to draw up water not running in defined channels underground, without being liable to compensation. The Bill would introduce a principle which would be dangerous- to colliery lessees. The common law principle which this Bill sought to alter was, in his opinion, founded upon justice and equity. If this Bill extended to goal proprietors they would be rendered responsible, notwithstanding the obliga- tions entered into by them, for many years to come. Eves if confined to one district it would be unjust and unfair. Water could not be taken from underground without re- moving some portion of the strata in solution. In reply to counsel fer the promoters, the witness said if they could begin with a clean sheet, with no obligations, and the law clearly defined, it might be right that compensation should be paid for subsidences. Mr. Durant, of the Geological Survey, then proceeded with his geological details of the salt beds of Cheshire.
