div.p: WINSFORD.

SCIENCE Smoot., WINSFORD.—Her Majesty's inspector of science schools having attended the Academy Science Classes during the week, expressed his pleasure at the arrangements and character of the students and the admirable manner in which the influential committee did their duty as superintendents of the Government examina- tions now being held.

THE SALT "TRADE.—The report for April is a fair average,though the Baltic Benson has been made very late by the severe winter. The ships being now free from the ice and arriving daily, the demand is improving as may be I seen from the prices which are being given for the salt. If I we look at the amounts sent to the United States for a period of seven years, no April exports exceed the past April, I reaching 21,796. To British America the amount is 14,787, which is much below, that of April last year, and somewhat below that of 1879 and 1877, but these were good years for the salt trade. To South America and the West Indies our export has been but about one-third of last April, Imo, though in excess of 1879, 1878, and 1875, yet the whole export during the year is much over any of the seven years, coming up to 6,202. Africa in last April took less (2,210) than in 1875, 1877, and 1880, but when joined to the previous exports it stands well. In the same way our East Indian exports for April are slightly below the same month last year, and much lower than in 1876, but for so much of the year it bears the best comparison. Our Ran- goon, dm., exports have risen immensely, showing that vast openings must have been made somewhere and by someone. To Australia we have sent less than in 1875, but more than in any April since, and up to this part of the year the four months stands well ;.while to the Prussian ports we did I much better in 1876, 1877, and 1880, and for the year a great decline when compared with the year 1876. Our Russian trade is so far lower as if a decline was in that quarter also, but after-months may make up for the ice bound season. Other Baltic and North Sea parts have done better except in 1880 and 1878, but may open out yet. The home trade stands fair,'but Holland is below any of the last seven years for April, bat not for the full four months of the year; the same may be said of Belgium. The total exports from the Mersey, which in 1880 reached 139,650, only came to 114,018 for last month, yet this is in advance of previous years, excepting last year. MAY DAY AT OVER AND WINSFORD.—This popular %a- tival was celebrated at Over and Winsford on Saturday last. The first of May being on the Sunday, it was more con- venient for the neighbourhood to hold the celebration ou the 7th 'nat., Saturday being generally a holiday. Mrs. Turner, of Over Hall, interested herself greatly in making it a suc- cess, in which she was assisted by a committee, Mr. Tolfree acting as secretary. Mrs. and the Misses Turner selected the queen and royal suite from the following schools, the scholars attending which, took part in the procession to the number of 1,400 or 1,500. Meadow Bank, and High-street Board schools, Waiver sobool, .14rnhall Grammar school, Over National school, and Whitegate school. The festivities were held in a field in Over, and the day was AS bright as could be wished. The town for some time before the procession started, presented quite a gala appearance. The children a.sembled in Mr. Cross's dockyard, and after being marshalled started in the following order. The Winsford Rifle Band, Ensign bearer, the above named schools, boys with banners, Maypole dancers very prettily dressed, two boys with crown and sceptre on cushions. The queen (a nice looking little girl, the daughter of Mr. Platt, of Ways Green) and her seven maids of honour. Lurries with pairs of horses, and carts with one horse, all the horses being gaily decorated. On arriving at the field Mrs. Turner ascended the throne and crowned the queen with a beautiful floral crown, and the band played The national anthem. Mr. Billington proposed ' a vote of thanks to MTS. and the Misses Turner for the great assistance they had rendered. Mrs. Turner responded saying she WAS glad to give happiness to the children, and pleased to see the festival such a success. The Maypole dance was executed very prettily by the children and must Lave cost the ladies above named some trouble to bring them to such perfection. Prizes were given for the best turnouts :-Ist Mr. Milling, waggoner, W. Saint; 2nd T. Knowles, Esq., M.P., waggoner, T. Baker; 3rd Mr. Rigby, waggoner, T. Davies; and Mr. Morton, of Morton Hall, a special prize. For the best horse and cart: Ist Mr. Billington, waggoner, G. Graham; 2nd Winsford stores, waggoner, T. Holbrook; and Mr. D. Wilson's waggoner a special prize. The judges were Mr. Henry Barnett, and Mr. Frith. Various games were in- dulged in, and the children had buns and milk. An im- mense number attended, and the festivities were quite a success in a pecuniary point of view. I ENTERTAINMENT AT WINSFORD.—An entertainment was given in the I oard Schools, Winsford, by the choir of the Primitive Chapel, Station-road, the proceeds of which were to be devoted to clearing off the debt on the Littler Chapel. The performance of the various songs, anthems, ck.c., was very creditable. Dr. Okell, the mayor, occupied the chair, and Alderman Hewitt took his place when he was called out. The attendance was very good. SACRED CONCERT AT WINSINPRD.—A concert was given in the Town Hall, Winsford, on Tuesday last, in aid of the funds fora new Wesleyan Chapel, the music being sacred and chiefly classical. Th 3 following amateurs took part : The Rev. C. Reader and the Misses Reader, and Mr. F. B. Cooke ; they were assisted by Mr. Singleton. The pro- gramme consisted of instrumental duets (piano and cabinet organ), songs, and vocal duets, which were all admirably rendered, and elicited much applause. The company was large and select, and the building fund would be increased by about £l9 or £2O.
. CKnisry's Mixs-rerms.—A band of minstrels occupied the Town Hall, Winsford, on Monday last, but the attendance would not pay expenses.

STORAGE OF ELECTRICITY FOR INDUSTRIAL AND Rolm Usx.—A new secondary battery, of greatly enlarged capa- city, is now attracting attention in Paris. It is the inven- tion of M. Faure, but is confessedly a development of the well-known secondary battery of M. Plante, which is formed of sheets of lead immersed in acidulated water. The latter gains in capacity as the process of charging and discharging is repeated, through increasing thickness of the layer of peroxide of lead that is slowly formed by the currents. M. Faure has conceived the idea of coating the two electrodes with layers of minium, or the red oxide of lead, and by this means the capacity is greatly increased. The Faure battery is stated to have forty times the power of accumulation of the Plante. A battery weighing 75 kilogrammes will de- velop 75 kilogrammetres or one-horse power, during one hour. As to the nature of the action, the electric current appears to change the minium to peroxide on the positive electrode, and to reduced lead on the negative. In dis- charging, the reduced lead is oxidised, and the peroxidised lead is reduced. The battery was lately exhibited by M. Reynier to the Society for Encouragement of National In- dustry. There were 24 couples weighing seven kilo- grammes each ; connected to a Siemens machine of medium size, these furnished a work of 47 kilogrammetres, which is 'about a third of M. Reyneir's figures; but the conditions paetent means ph oyfs ictlrs were unfavourable. Next, a hand of platinum, three metres long, 12 millimetres broad, and four-tenths of a millimetre ibspueatinkg hope- fully thick was made to glow; then two incandescence-lamps were lighted. The superiority to the Plante battery was fwuellllydoefmision. ystraaut demonstrated. elec- tricity to any house or workshop independently of others Some ercy competent that may be supplied, and free from the drawbacks of a system of canalisation. The method is also regarded as very promising for domestic electric lighting. A company, it may be added, has been lately started in Paris by M. philippart, for obtaining force and light by electricity, by combination of the.Reynier and Faure batteries. M. Hos- pitaller has pointed out the expensiveness of charging the Faure battery with electricity from chemical action.

SPECIAL SERVICES IN THE CIRCUS. Sir,—Would you kindly allow me space to crrrect a Statement made in the Borough Court, on Monday Ist, by Mr. Moore, on behalf of Mr. Harroston, viz., that no change! Would be made for the use of the circus for the above services. The committee wish it to be known th3t this statement is not correct, and as the expenses will be nut by \ voluntary contributions (if left unnoticed), might prevent their receiving the necesssary support from the public to suable them to carry on this work. Mr. Harms.on has treated the committee with every consideration ; but to ex- pect him to give the circus, gas, and men to look after his property for nothing would he unreasonable. Trusting you will be able to find room for this correction, and oblige, /ours faithfully, 77, Manchester-road. A. SMITH, Hon. Sec.
FRINGING THE RIGHTS OF RUNCORN FREE. HOLDERS. "

"The price of liberty is eternal vigilance." Sir,—The question which Mr. Frith asked at the last meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, with regard to the inclosing of a portion of common land, on the Weston-read, is one fraught with interest to the public at Large. It is only right that the Commissioners, as the representatives of the public, 'should take the steps they have; and I can only regret that action was not taken sooner. It must have been patent to numbers of people, for some time past, that a palpable infringement of the public rights was being carried on, for iron fencing has not yet acquired the powers of mushroom growth, nor can stone gate pillars rise by magic. Of course, they can be made to disappear in a very short space of time. The plan which our fathers were in the habit of periodically adopting, viz.: and literally "riding rough-shod" walking the boundary over the com non land in the neighbourhood, to ascertain if UV encro Lchrnents bad been made by greedy "land- grabbers" and if so, to tear down the fences, and root up the growing produce, without ceremony, is one wkich it is worth while to consider about reviving. In the case under discussion I believe potatoes have been sown. Now, the best plan to adopt with regard to the crop of potatoes would be to allow them to ripen, and when they are "got," to have them seat to Dalton Workhouse with the compliments of the Runcorn free-holders, under the care of Mr. Lowe, with a request that in future the Master's pony may not be refused a few "boiled potatoes." If the little farce could end so happily it would be a " consummatioq devoutly to be wished." But front the dogged pertinacity of the individual charged with enclosing the land in question, and his supercilious demeanour when taken to task by the town surveyor, we may expect to have a lively time of it before a settlement has been arrived at. The fact that he is not totally unconnected with the law adds no little to the difficulty. Such practices must be nipped in the bud, or there is no telling what the abuse may grow into. If every man who has smelt parchment, and fancies on the strength of it that he can drive a "coach and four" through an Act of Parliament, goes in for a patch of common land there will not be a breathing place left in a district already well- nigh as stifling as a second edition of the last days of Sodom and Gomorrah. Hoping some energetic defender of the rights of the people will take this question up in the colemns of the Examiner —a paper which has done yeoman service in purifying to a large extent the public officialism of the town—l beg to subscribe myself Yours truly, Runcorn, May 10th, 1881. NEMESIS.

COUNTY COURT CURIOSITIES. Dear Sir,—At the County Court held the other day, the following case came before the judge. An agent on behalf of a landlord sued a tenant for balance of rent owing as arrears, after he had left the house. Judge: Does the defendant *we you the money ?_Agent: No your honour, it is owing —landlord.—Judge: I am afraid I can't hear you.— Agent: But your honour, if the landlord were here he could Sot help us in the matter, not having had anything what- ever to do with the case. I am his agent, and as such he has left it entirely with me to carry it through.—Judge: Yes. But I can't bear you in the absence of the landlord.— Agent (surprised and a little excited): Then am I and other agents to understand that in future you refuse to hear us on behalf of plaintiff.—Judge: Quite so.—Agent: Then sir, suppose I were to have a tenant removing, leaving an arrear of 25., and the owner livirg at Crewe or a similar distance (as I have several) in a ease like that, should I be allowed to appear as agent, or would it be absolutely neces- sary fer the landlord to appear personally.—Judge : I could not hear you.—Agent: But your honour,the person to whom I refer in Crewe holds a very impogant position as a public man, and would not think of loosing time and suffering such a loss, to appear here for the paltry sum of 25.—Judge: You must take the course open to you.—The case was then struck out, but the fee paid for entrance was retained by the court as usual. Notice was sent to the , agent this week that he had to pay 4s. for expenses to defendant by 2nd of May. Can anyone inform me why this I plan of dealing with agents is adopted, and what is the oourse referred to by the judge ?—No. 2. This was for a balance of £ll Os. Bid. due for lent money, on September 12, 1877. The plaintiff in this case lent defendant £3O upon promissory `Nut default was made by defendant in the repayments, left a balance of £ll Os. Eild. owing. This was entarau into the County Court February 19, 1879. The court fees paid on that occasion for entrance and hearing was £1 175., and the judges then gave judgment for payment in 14 days. Defendant, however, though a thorough business man, and recently an owner of property, did not ply anything. Some time afterwards an execution was taken out against his furniture, court fees this time being 19s. 6d. This was money lost again so far, for he bad changed his residence, gone to Liverpool, and put a son's name over the door. The plaintiff, in order to get full satisfaction to meet the requirements of the judge, I had to make two special journeys to Liverpool which of course cost money and time. He, however, suc- ceeded in getting the particulars required from defendant's daughter, that her father was there and at work. A judge- ment summons was then taken out, paying a court fee this time of 45., but the summons was returned as not served. On plaintiff stating so emphatically that defendant was there, it was sent to Liverpool a second time but only to be re- turned again with the same reply—" had not found him." The plaintiff feeling a little annoyed at this delay, asked the court to allow him to serve defendant personally, but was soon told by the officials there could be no further efforts made to serve that summons for the same fee, but if plaintiff wished to press the case he could do so and be allowed to serve the summons at his own expense and upon payment of another court fee of 45. The plaintiff thinks, and no doubt the public will see through the same spectacles, that this is paying very heavily for the piper, for it stands thus to re- cover a debt of £ll Os. M.. there has been already paid to the court for lets a total Of just £3. The next payment for entrance alone will be 45., which will make a total of £3 45., without having recovered et en one penny toward the debt. What this case will cost at this rate of procedure it is dif- tcult to say, but one thing is certain that this plaintiff like all tha rest, if he intends doing his best to recover the debt, is simply to continue paying and waiting. But this is very poor satisfaction for a business man after he has lent his money, or let out goods, to be put to all this annoyance and expense to get what legally belongs to him: for in many cases—if even be succeeds in recovering the debt—the time lost alone is a greater loss than the debt itself would have been. These are two cases out of a many. I would like to have brought another matter before the public, but fearing to trespass upon your valuable paper, and not having a moment of time to spare, prefer to leave it for another issue.— Remaining, dear sir, yours, A SUFFERER.

CHESHIRE SALT DISTRICTS COMPEN- SATION BILL. The Cheshire Salt Districts Compensation Bill, promoted by property owners in Northwich and Winsford, asking that provisions might be made for the assessment, levy, and application of compensation for damage by subsidence of land in the salt districts of Cheshire, came again on Mon- day before a hybrid Committee of the House of Commons, consisting of Sir Sydney Waterlow (chairman), Hon. E. L. Stanley, Viscount Emlyn, Mr. Storey-Maskelyne, Sir Hy. Tyler, Colonel St. John Berne, and Mr.Blennerhassett. Mr. Pope, Q.C., Mr. Michael, Q.C., and Mr. R. S. Wright appeared for the promoters; Mr. Pember, Q.C., and Mr. Balfour Brown for the salt proprietors; Mr. Salisbury for owners of property in the salt districts; Sir E. Beckett, Q.C., and Mr. Higgin, Q.C., for the River Weaver Naviga- tion Trustees; and Mr. J. W. Batten for the Wheelock Iron and Salt Company. The cross-examination of Mr. Thomas Ward, manager of the salt works of Messrs. Ashton and Sons, Northwich, was continued by Mr. Balfour Brown. Witness said that there was a large area of land at Northwich that had gradually sunk during the last 20 years although it had not shown any signs of rupture by subsidence. In a portion or the Northwich district attempts had been made to obtain brine, but it had not been found in sufficient quantity to make the works profitable. The largest pumper of brine in Northwich was Mr. Townsend, whose works produced about 200,000 tons of salt a year. Outbursts of water, containing a large proportion of salt, had taken place at Winsford so recently as 1879. The Chairman asked the witness whether the brine was above or below the working standard. The Witness said the brine was fully saturated, although he did not test it. It was the result of an enormous laud slip of some 60,000 or 70,000 tons of earth. The brine was 80 yards below the surfa when this took place. In reply to Sir E. Beckett, witness said that he did not know a single case where property was sold subject to risks of subsidence, or where the risk was distinctly stated. Has there been an instance within your knowledge where anyone has been called upon to pay compensation for damage done by subsidence? It has not been done because there has been no possibility of getting at any particular individual. The Weaver Company in one instance were asked for compensation, not, he believed, as a matter of right, but on the ground that they derived a large profit from the salt trade, which they spread all over the country without doing any benefit to the district injured. By Mr. Lyulph Stanley: The Worcestershire salt trade was capable of expansion if there were convenient ports for export purposes. He was aware of the German system in operation at Nancy, of putting fresh water into shafts sunk down to work salt beds, and then pumping up the brine created by the dissolution of the bed. It was possible by that method to limit the damage to the particular locality. That system did not exist in Cheshire. If that system was adopted the manufacturer ought to be exempted from the tax, if he could prove that he had so restricted his opera- tions. The difficulty was that the tendency of the water was to get behind the shaft and eat away the rock salt, and if that took place there would be a danger of the natural water flowing in. The withdrawal from Cheshire of 300,000 or 400,000 tons of the salt would doubtless affect some of the manufacturers of the district, but it would not necessarily make an alteration in the prices charged by those ' who remained. Re-examined by Mr. Wright: He did not think that the maximum tax of 3d. per ton would be required. The full I tax would produce about £20,000 a year, but he believed that ld. or fit would be a sufficient tax at present. Upon that basis he estimated that the amount available next year would be about £B,OOO, which would allow a reserve for a sinking fund. The German system of pumping could not, in his opinion, be advantageously adopted in Cheshire. There would he no objection to exempt any manufacturer from the tax who adopted it. Mr. Edward Leader Williams, consulting engineer, Man- chester, and formerly engineer to the River Weaver Naviga- tion Trustees, and the Bridgewater Trustees, who was next examined by Mr. Michael, said that in his opinion the area of the salt stratification in Cheshire was about twenty miles from north-west to south east, and fifteen miles across from north-eat to south-west. The deposits of ',salt were practi- cally inexhaustible, but there was no doubt that the subsi- dences of land were due to the pumping of brine. There were fifty-two pumpw at work in the district, twenty-four being at Winsford and eighteen in Northwich. Those at Winsford were within a mile of each other. If the 24 at Winsford were kept continually pumping up brine the ab- straction of the diaaolYed mineral substratum must lead to a sinking of the surface levels. He thought that the marl above the rock salt broke up into fissures, through which the rain could pass. As a result of this there would be a dis- solution of the salt, but no matter whatever quantity of rain so penetrated, the effect on the level of the land would be infinitesimal, as compared with the results of pumping. There were only two causes apart from the pumping which would tend to the further solution of the rock salt if the water were fully saturated with brine. The first would be the law of diffusion—fresh water entering and being carried off as brine; the second would be hydraulic pressure forcing out the brine. Neither of these causes could have produced the results which had followed from the pumping. There was no such hydraulic pressure as would drive up enough brine to cause subsidence. If there had been the subsidence would have occurred before the pumps were established. Similar results had occurred in Droitwich, where a small salt manufacture was carried en. The towing path of the river Weaver, just outside Northwich, had fre- quently subsided, and hadhad to be raised at different times. Several weirs and lakes had also been destroyed on the Weaver by the subsidence that had taken place. The pro- perty in Northwich had been considerably damaged, the magistrates's room being in a very dangerous state. The magistrates occasionally met in the Court-room, but they generally preferred to meet in a drill shed outside the town. The damage was still going on at Winsford. In hia opinion the maximum tax of 3d. per ton would not be required unless some exceptional landslips took place, but even if it was there was not the slightest reason to suppose that the salt trade of Cheshire would' be affected by the competition of other districts. By the Chairman: The-trade of the river Weaver was principally due to the manufacture of salt in Cheshire. By Mr. Storey-Maskelyne He was unable to say at what distance from the pumping stations he could ttace the flow of the brine, but he could trace the subsidence for two By the Chairman: A district should only pay tompensa• tion according to the quantity of salt abstracted. Cross-examined by Mt. Higgin : Therm were a number of landowners in Cheshire who pumped brine, and sold it to the salt makers in large quantities. There were some manufac- turers who both pumped and bought brine. There was no proposal in the bill to tax the landowners. It was more convenient to collect the tax from the pumper. The committee then adjourned. On Tuesday Mr. G. L. Williams, civil engineer, Manches- ter, who was under examination when the committee ad- journed on Monday, stated, in answer to further questions, that he was of opinion that the ordinary law was insufficient for the protection of property, inasmuch as it was impos- sible to ascertain which brine shaft the damage was caused by. In reply to Mr Salisbury, the witness added that the Congregational Chapel at Northwich was coming down through sulasidence. The site had been sold and turned into auction-rooms, but he had not heard that it had been sold for more money than it was originally bought for. He thought the area of the districts unnecessarily large, and he waa in favour of curtailing them. Mr. George F. Wilbraham, of Delmore Rouse, Wiasford, was next called and examined by Mr. Michael. He stated that he was a juatite of the peace for Cheshire, chairman of the Northwichßoard of Guardians, and one of the River Weaver trustees. He was the owner of some 4,000 or 5.000 acres of land in the townships of Over, Weaver, and Clive, which had suffered considerably from ;subsidence. At the present time there was a large "flash "'of water at Weaver which, forty-five years ago, was dry lsnd, and there was a considerable quanti'y of land partially submerged. For- merly there was a bridge opposite Weaver Hall, and that had had to be removed in consequence of subsidence, while four or five years ago he had to construct a new road from Winsford to Weaver, the old one having sunk and become flooded by water frem the " flash " he hadrnentioned. From time to- time his residence at Weaver had had to be repaired in con- sequence of cracks in the walls. The greater portion of the township of Weaver had suffered from the subsidence. Wit- ness derived no benefit from the Winsford Balt trade, but owned salt works on the other side of the county, between Lawton and Wheelock. He thought it was only right that compensation should be made to those persons whose pro- perties suffered from subsidence. weßreYnMotrPet supportinge salt works. the ev ebriai , large thleayndwowerneearlslitnhethoewncrifrsrioeft very much injured by subsidence. He had actually under By the Chairma n.—Witness's property a Weaver had been zen up by water and pirtially under water something like a bun re acres, in addition to a great deal more that was bra d fissures in the ground. bridge master, examined by Mr. Wright, stated let bridges Mr. Stanhope Balt, county surveyor for Cl:eshire,. and at Winsford, Northwich, and Witton had had to, be raised sequence of sulasidence caused, as he believed, by brine at great expense from time to time in recent years in con- pumping. The new police station at Northwieh was erected in 1875, on what was supposed to be safe ground, but the walls had badly cracked, and had to be,' pinned through" Several times. The building would have tube abandoned the sinking continued. On the Committee rewming on Wednesday, Igv..Heckett,bniide4Plczthwioh and Huttcrd, said he bo.l

had large experience in rating property. During the forty years over which his knowledge extended great damage had been caused by subsidence, and more especially within the last ten years. He had made an examination of the damage caused by settling in Northwich and the immediate district. The value of the property was £311,835, and the gross depreciation was £102,945. The annual loss in repairs and maintenance was £5,147, but if the subsidence increased the loss yearly would increase. Fire insurance premiums were raised in consequence of the use of timber in building. In Northwich and district 5 public buildings, 15 manufactories, 21 stables, 34 workshops, 41 public-houses, 140 shops, and 640 houses were affected by the subsidence. In one year after a building was erected it would begin to show signs of cracking, though it might not be necessary to rebuild it. The Town Hall at Winsford was raised Sit. fin, in 1879. He did not think the bill would injuriously affect the salt trade. In reply to Mr. Higgin' the witness said that he did not I think that a pumper of brine should be taxed. The bill ought only to apply to the person who manufactured salt, though he did not actually do the mischief. Mr. Devonport, land surveyor, stated that he had made a valuation of the property in the Winsford district. About 644 acres of land had been injured by subsidence. He esti- mated the value of property in the Winsford district in its present damaged condition at £127,621 or £40,037 less than it would have been but for the subsidences. The loss to owners in reduced rents and repairs he set down at £1,579 10s. per annum. He had no doubt that the subsi- dences were caused by pumping of brine. Mr. James Cowley, clerk to the Northwich Local Board, proved the rateable value of the several portions of the Northwich district affected by subsidences, and ex- plained that the Local Board bad been compelled to put in force their exceptional powers with regard to dangerous buildings in ten cases, and had been put to an expense of £335 for special repairs to roads owing to the same cause. Mr. Ludwig Mond, one of the managing directors of the firm of Brunner, Mond, and Co., alkali manufacturers, North- wich, stated that at the works brine was used in the manu- facture of alkali under a patent, which he had the right of using. Other manufacturers used common salt. The firm were the promoters of the bill. In his opinion a tax of 3d. per ton would not injure the salt trade in connection with the manufacture of alkali. As pump.rs of brine his firm would have to pay a considerable proportion of the compen- sation if the bill were passed. He attributed the subsidences in a great measure to the brine pumping. Mr. Henry Neumann' 'a justice of the piece and guardian of the poor at Northwhich, and also a pumper of brine at Marston, gave evidence as to damage caused to his residence by subsidence. It was partially rebuilt ten or eleven years ago, and the whole of it now required rebuilding. Until recently, the nearest brine shaft to his house was about two miles distant. He had been a merchant in Liverpool, and, having exported very large quantities of salt, he was of opinion that the proposed tax would not have the slightest effect on the trade. The price of salt was at present low, and, as it varied daily, the manufacturers would easily re- coup themselves. Northwich was the centre of an agricul- tural district, and, without being dependent on the salt trade, might be a flourishing town. The committee again adjourned.

div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

LANCASHIRE:A dull tone generally prevails throughon the coal trade of this district, with an easing down in the price of classes of round coal. So far as house-fire classes of coal are concerned businesss is rapidly relapsing into the usual summer trade, and both at the Manchester collieries, which up to the present time have been kept fully going with, orders, and at pits in other districts stocks are accumulating, with short time coming more generally into operation. As the falling off in the demand for house-fire coals is accompanied with a continued very limited inquiry for the commoner sorts for ironmaking and general manu- facturing purposes, a weakness generally is imparted b the market, although there has been no further alteration of list rates beyond those already announced. Sellers, however, in many cases are being compelled under pressure to take less money, and for common round coals, which are rather a drug in the market, very low prices are ruling. The better qualities of round coal for house-fire purposes are to be bought at the pit mouth at about Ss. 6d. to Ps.; seconds, at 6s. 9d. to 78.3 d.; and common round coals at from ss. 3d. to 58. 9d. per ton. Any actual firmness in the market is confined to engine classes of fuel, and although at present no material advance is being obtained generally, burgy hnd slack are being held for fully late rates, with a tendency to stiffen. Good steam burgy fetches readily about 4s. 6d. to 58., and good slack 4s. to 4s. 6d. per ton at the pit, with a trifle more being asked for some special sorts. Collieries here and there are tolerably well supplied with shipping orders, but this branch of trade is generally quiet, with low prices ruling, steam coal, delivered at either Liverpool or or Garston being, in some cases, offered at under 7s. per ton. The iron market continues extremely dull, and for pig and manufactured iron the inquiry during the week has again been of the most limited description. .An absence of any actual requirements rather than any question of prices ap- pears tube the chief cause of the depression, and in the face of the decided weakness on the part of sellers, dealers are not inclined to speculate for forward delivery. Lancashire makers of pig iron are still asking 448. to 455. per ton, less 21. per cent. for forge and foundry qualities delivered into the Manchester district, but only limited sales are being made; these, however, are still being helped up with deliveries on account of old contracts which keep the local furnaces going. In outside brands of pig iron where any basiness is being done in this market it is at lower prices, and Lincolnshire forge iron has been sold at as low as 425. per ton, less 21- for delivery, equal to Manchester. In the position of finished iron makers there is no material change to notice, and where forges are kept busy it is chiefly on old orders. Except for shipment very few new inquiries are coming in, and prices continue low, ordinary bars delivered into the Manchester district averaging about £5 129. 6d. to £5 158. Eng;neers as a rule are only moderately employed, and amongst the large machinists in the district less wok is reported in hand.

div.head: LECTURE AT MARSHALL'S CROSS, ST. HELENS.
div.p: LECTURE AT MARSHALL'S CROSS, ST. HELENS.

"IT'S ALL A MATTER OF TASTE." On Tuesday evening, the Rev. H. J. Weatherhead delivered an interesting lecture on the above subject, in the United Methodist Free Church, :Marshall's Cross. Mr. John Smith of Cloc-k Face, occupied the chair. The attendance was not very good, but the audience proved to be a very appreciative one.

The LECTURER said the phrase, "It's all a, matter ot taste," was so constantly in use, and its signification was so well understood, that he should not need to spend much time in explaining its meaning. He referred to a few different ways in which the word "taste" might be legitimately used and understood. He supposed they were all more or less familiar with that sense of the word which referred to per- ception by the tongue and palate of the flavour of that which entered the mouth; and he gave two or three amusiog storiesillustrative of certain people's ideas as to what would suit the tastes of sickly men. In concluding his-remarks on this-portion of the lecture, he gave a little advice as to the observance of the laws of health, remarking that if they wanted to keep an unperrerted taste and a good appetite, together with a thoroughly sound digestion, they must observe those plain unalterable laws which God had estab- lished as the environment of physical life of man; thus the avoidance of all irregularities of living, such as indulgence in the luxuries of the table, eating too much, too frequently or too quickly, or on the other hand, too long abstinence from food, too little out-of-door exercise, excessive bodily or mental exerxion, late hours, or exposure to cold and damp, He also recommended total abstinence from intoxicants as a means of preservirg good health. Sometimes the word was used to signify an essay, a trial, or an experiment. They would sometimes hear people speak about something which they bad tried, or essayed to do, and theywould say, "I have just had a taste of it." He dared say some of them bad had a taste of the rod in their young days. It was never very popular with them at that time, but he had no doubt it did them a great deal of good. The 'old' adage told them that those who spare- the rod spoil the "chiltk,;. and although he never was an advocate for excessive or severe punishment, and was scarcely likely to be now that he-bad children of his own, yet he was- inclined to believe that there was no lesson that was likely to be of more practi- cal use to a person in the battle of life than the lesson Of obedience to authority, the lesson of bending the will to a superior power, and acknowledging the authority existing therein. The restraints of home induence aad parental authority were too frequently cast aside as a burdensome and unnecessary thing, and children of tender years asaamed an independence of parental control which he never dared to take upon himself during all the time he resided at home, and he had the great advantage of remaining theta until the attainment of his twentieth year. Ij the habit of obedience to authority were more frequently encouraged and developed there would not be so fearful a record of crime and wrong doing, as they were at present sadly too familiar with. Another and perhaps pita equally important sense in which he purposed using the word taste, related to choice. He dare say thay had sometimes used these words " Ics all a matter of taste, as the woman said when she kissed the cow." Of course :t was, and perhaps:the cow thought a; as well ; be was not going to blame the woman. If a person delibsrately chose pleasures, ornaments, and pastimes that were rile and vicious, or pursuits that showed that he had no relish for the beautiful and sublime, he was said to have bad taste; whereat, if he preferred thoae things that were pure and trees and of good report, and that had a tendency to exalt and ennoble human nature, they unhesitatingly credit him with good taste. The eholce that was made depends upon this intellectual relish or discernment existing.in the min and thus became the indication of the possession of either good or bad taste. It was very wonderful bow much de- pended upon the choice they made from day to day. Wha. t man liked that would be seek after, and the principle applied to every department of life which it was possible to cons ider The determination of our minla was quickened and inten!! a fled by companlonsbip. The subject was capable of appli- cation to, the relationships the domestic circle. It wasal a matter of taste that decided whetner their homes weree he l g abodes of quietness, and comfort, and peace, or thedw..t.n places of strife, and unrest, and confusio;i . I SUDDEN DEATH AT ST. HELENS.—On Wednesday after- noon Mr. Driffield, the district coroner, held an inquest on on the body of Margaret Hay, 92, Duke-street, aged 43 years, who died suddenly on Sunday morning. Deceased had en- joyed good health, and her sudden death caused great con- sternation in the neighbourhood. " Death from natural causes" was the verdict of the jury. PRESCOT CATTLE AND PIO FAIRS.—TIC last of the Prescot cattle and pig fairs for this year, took place on Tuesday. The show of cattle was about the same as on last fair day, the stock including principally cows of the milk- ing and store kinds. A few young bulls were also offered. Very few sales were effected in any kind. Good store cattle realised from £lO to £l7, and milking cows brought , from £l5 to £25. There were alSo a few pigs on sale, but tha sale was (mkt, FOOT-AND-I'lam bisEask, NElat PRESCOT.—On Tues- day, an outbreak of this disease was reported on the farm of Mr. Manly Spink, of Westfield House, Knotty Ash; near I Present, two cows out of a herd of three being affected, and 27 pigs out of a herd of 53. Several other outbreaks are re- ported in various parts of the county. In consequence, the , coming fairs at Newton and Leigh will not be held. Of the , six fairs that should have taken place at Prescot this year, only two could be held owing to the disease. PEESCOT POL/CE COURT.—At this court on Monday, before Mr. W. L. Evans, John Gellis, of Liverpool, was brought up on remand charged with having at Tarbuck races, lon Saturday, the 23rd ult., stolen a silver watch, value £6, from the person of Francis Briggs, of Clive-hall farm, York- shire. The case was adjourned from the previous Tuesday, for the production of a witness, who pointed out the prisoner as the person who stole the watch. The police now stated that diligent search had 'been made for the witness, but she could not be found, owing to her having given a wrong ad- dress. Mr. Evans remanded the prisoner till next Tuesday, intimating that if the witness was not found in the mean- time the prisoner would have to be discharged.—George Walton, John O'Neil, John Merphy,James Evans, and Mary Evans were brought charged with stealing and receiving a rrtmber of articles, consisting of knives and forks, towels, bottles of champagne and claret, silver spoons, silver cups, Zc., the property of Mr. John Pigott, of Grassendale-park, Grarston. The property in question was left by the owner in, his private carriage at Tarbock racecource, on the 23rd ult whilst be and a party went to witness a race. On returning Mr. Pigott missed the articles' and he at once gave informa- tion to the police, which led to the apprehension of the prisoners.—liemanded till Tuesday, ROBBEET AT Ifurrox.—On Monday last, information was received at the Prescot Police Office, that sometime 'be- tween half-past five o'clock on the evening, of the Bth inst., and a quarter-past six o'clock on the evening of the '9th inst., a black cloth coat, value £2, had been stolen from the dwellingThouse of William 'Orford, a labourer, residing on the Liverpool-road, near The Hazels, Huyton. Early on Monday afternoon, P.S. Spinits, whilst on duty at Warring- ton, met two boys named dames Bart and William Henry Lewisone of whom was wearing a coat which seemed much too large for him. The officer's suspicions being aroused, be stopped and questioned them, 'but their renlics not being satisfactory he took theni to the-police offics, were they admitted that they had absconded from the Holy Trinity Industrial School, Grafton-street, 'Toxteth- park, Liverpool, and that whilst on their way to Warrington Burt entered Orford's house and stole the coat. Informa- tion was sent to the school authorities at Liverpool, and on the-same evening the boys were handed over to two of the officials. Burl, who had previously absconded twice, was given into custody, and on Tuesday was brought up at the ,Dale-street police court, before Mr. Raffles, charged with absconding with the clothing of the institution, and re- manded for seven days. 'Lewis, who, it appeared, had been led away by the other prisoner, was taken back into the institution. On Tuesday;P.S. Stevens, stationed at Huyton, in company with the man'Orford, went to 'Warringtonovhere the latter recognised the coat found on the boys as the one stolen from his house, and it was accordingly handed over to him.

PRESCOT RURAL DEANERY.—A conference of the mem- bers of the Rural Deanery of Prescot was held on Wednesday in the grand jury room, St. Georges Hall, Liverpool, under the presidency of the Rev. W. L. Feilden, the rural dean. The proceeding were opened with prayer, after which the conference proceeded to the election .of the committees and secretaries. In the Committee of Selection, the clerical members were re-elected, as were also the lay members with the exception that Mr. Bartlett was -snbstituted for Mr. Hornby ; and the secretaries were re-appointed. Canon Pen- rhyn was.appointed clerical and Col. Wyatt and Mr. Gambia lay representatives on the management committee for a dio- cesan conference. 'From the treasurer'estatement of accounts it appeared that the receipts for the pastyear were £4 18s. ed. which included a balance of 18s. ; and the expenditure for the same time was £4 Os. 6d. The Rev. Charles Barr, of All Saints', West Derby, then read a paper on the Church Boards Bill, which was introduced into Parliament this ses- sion. Mr. Barr caid he had no hesitat'on in appealing to them as to whether the bill wee not only wild but unfelr. After consideris.lg a number of points in the bill, Mr. Barr said the only amendment he cock' propose in it was that the word "not" should be inserted in the first line of the bill, and it would then read, "Be it pot enacted." (Applause.) A discussion iollowed, in the course of which the Rev. Canon Carr said, speaking-as a cCergyman, be thought they had been too jealous of lay assistance, and suggested that a parochial council might be formed by increasing the num- ber of sidesmen.—The proceedings were brought to a close with the usual vote of thanks to the chairman.

THE FATHER OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.— On Tues- day was the 78th anniversary of the birth of Mr. Christopher Rice Manse! Talbot, M.P., and Lord Lieutenant of Glamorganshire, who was born on May 10, 1808. Mr. Talbot is the sen of the late Mr. Thomas Mangel Talbot, of Margam Park, Glamorganshire, by his marriage with Lady Mary Lucy Fox Strangways, daughter of Henry Thomas, second Earl of Ilchester. Mr. Talbot has represented Glamorganshire in the House of Commons since /830, having thus had a seat in Parliament for upwards of half a century, and is the only member of that body who voted at the passing of the Reform Bill in 1832. A peerage was offered to this gentleman in 1869, but he declined the honour.

div.head: NCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: NCORN BURIAL BOARD.
ti

The CHAIRMAN read several letters, amongst which was one from Mrs. Eliza Barrow, thanking the Board for their Lind vote of condolence in her sudden bereavement. RESIGNATION OF MR. WELLS. A letter was read by the Chairman from Mr. I. J. Wells, dated the 10th inst., stating that owing to circumstances which were beyond his control, he felt it desirable he should resign his seat at the Board. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which were approved on thomotion of Mr. Gaskell, seconded by Mr. Gossage, stated that the quantity of water delivered during the four weeks ending the 20th ult., had been 40,708,893 gallons, as com- pared with 40,384,158 gellons for 1880, or an increase of 324.735 gallons for the present year. The quantity in stock was 11,602,809 gallons. The gas sent out during the same period had been 5,415,000 cubic feet, as compared with 5,433,000 cubic feet for the last year—a decrease of 18,000 cubic feet—or .33 per cent. The illuminating power of the gas bad been 16.74 candles. The Law-Clerk sub- mitted the draft of an agreement with Mr. Timmins, relative to the proposed works in substitution for the works remain- ing to be executed under Mr. Timmins's contract of Septem- ber, 1877. This having been considered and revised in con- ference with the last-named gentleman, the committee had subject to the inspection of Mr. reaolved to approve of it, Gosaage. HIGHWAY column-ma—AMENDING A TENDER.—THE WIRRINGTON-ROAD SCHOOLS' PAYING. The minutes of the Highway, Building, and Street Com- mittee, stated that the question of retaining the services of Mr. Copeland, sarveyor to the sewerage scheme—it not having been decided to immediately proceed with the work —had been considered, and the surveyor had stated that Mr. Copeland's time was fully occupied, and he could not be spared. Resolved, that the attention of the Board be called to the terms of agreement with the Leigh estate, requiring the commencement of the sewerage works prior to the Ist of July next. Resolved that the surveyor be instructed to examine and re- port as to the beet mode of making good the asphalted por- tion of the tootwalk on the easterly side of Victoria-road. Mr. James Taylor, of Liverpool, and Mr. Rimmer, architect, waited upon the committee respecting Peel House-lane widening, and Mr. Taylor offered to give up all the land re- quired for the improvement from a point marked Aon the plan in Peel House lane, to Bin Mill-lane, in consideration of the Board kerbing and cindering the footwalk and paying the architect for the cost of altering the plans. The com- mittee recommended that the proposal should be accepted. A deputation from the Runcorn Property and Investment Co., consisting of Messrs. P. Speakman, Pritchard, and All- card interviewed the Board, as to the proposed widening of Lower House lane. The deputation agreed to the improve- ment line shown of the plans passed by the Board, being carried out only subject to their (the Board) bricking the footpath in addition to kerbing, when the property was built, and the committee recommended the adoption of this pro- posal. Tenders as to the flagging at Simm's-cross Board Schools in Widnes and Milton-roads were received from Messrs. Lee and Co. ot Ditton, Messrs. Baron and Brooks, Mr. Daniel Hirst, Messrs. Roberts, Bros., and Mr. Thomas Sadler, Widnes, and it was resolved that the tender of Mr. Daniel Hirst, to execute the works for the sum of £93 19s. 6d. being the lowest, be recommended for acceptance. Tenders had been received as to paving streets at Warrington-road Board Schools from J. Lee and Co., Carter and Winter, Baron and Brooks, Thomas Sadler, and Daniel Hirst. It was resolved that the tender of Mr. Daniel Hirst, to do th e work for • the sum of £6lO (being the lowest), be recommended for ac- ceptance. The surveyor was instructed to serve the builders in the town with a notice that the Board would be strict in re- quiring plans of building to be submitted and approved before they were commenced. Mr. KERSHAW moved, and Mr. Pawiturrnsr seconded a motion in favour of the adoption of the minutes. Mr. BEEFS proposed, and Mr. GOSSAGE seconded an amendment, referring the proposal as to the paving of the foothpath at Warrington-road Schools back for re- consideration. Mr. GASICELL said that it was decided some time ago, that the work of the Board should be done by contract as far as possible, and he wished to know if the adoption of this plan had resulted in any reduction of the staff. Mr. KERSHAW explained that since the acceptance of the tender for the work at Warrington-road schools by Mr. D. Hirst, that gentleman had sent in an amended tender. Mr. BEASLEY said Mr. Hirst stated in his communication, that he had made a mistake in working out the estimate which had been accepted, and he could not now undertake the wo-k under £648 17s. 10d. Mr. KERSHAW said he proposed to go carefully into the question of the possibility of reducing the staff, with the surveyor. As to Mr. Copeland, the surveyor stated that tbet ofßolal was fully employed. They certainly needed some one to do the work, which Mr. Copeland was at present carrying out. The CHAIRMAN felt it to be his duty to call the attention of the Board to the fact, that unless the sewerage scheme were proceeded with prior to the Ist July, they were under a bond to pay the sum of £2,312. He proposed to bring this subject before their notice fully at the next meeting, in order that they might decide whether the work should be gone on with or not. The sewering of the town must certainly be proceeded with sooner or later, and £2,312 seemed to be a large sum to pay for not proceeding with it. The amendment was put and passed by a large majority, after which the minutes were passed with this alteration. HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. The minutes of the Health Committee were approved, on the motion of Mr. CAREY, seconded by Mr. BANICHURST. The Medical Officer's report showed that during April there had been 87 births, or a rate of 41.7 per 1,000 of the popu- lation ; and 38 deaths, or 18.2 per 1,000. The deaths in- cluded those of nine children under one year of age, and eleven between one and five years. Three people had died from zymotic diseases, and five inquests had been held. Mr. Dickson's report showed that during April there had been one fatal case of scarlet fever and two of measles. Owing to further complaints from the St. Patrick's school teachers and others, the inspector had, in company with the medical officer, called at Mr. Glover's works. That gentleman wished the Board to defer the action until Whitsuntide, and he promised that at that time he would raise his chimney several feet with the object of remedying the nuismce. In the meantime he would do all he could to prevent its recurrence. In company with the surveyor, the inspector had examined the drainage of water closets and urinals at the Central station, and found them most defective in construction and condition. The surveyor had been directed to write to the engineer of the railway companies, asking that an appointment should be made at the station in order that some arrangement might be made for remedying the state of matters.—The auditor having surcharged the amounts paid to Dr. Cooper, on account of salary for the years 1879-80, on the ground of an informality in the ap- pointment oftamedical officer, the law clerk was instructed to take steps terEave the matter put right and the surcharges remitted.—The law clerk having presented an account from Mantra Price. WoOdcock and Co., solicitors to Greenough's Trustees, of their ch irgee in connection with the negotiations for the purchase of the slaughterhouse site (which fell through) lie was instructed to have such charges taxed by the proper officer.—The alternative plan as to Halton- view drainage, submitted by the surveyor, having been in- spected and conseed it was recommended that the origi- nal plan be ad op ent—and the surveyor be instructed to submit it, and an estimate of its cost to the next Board meeting. FINANCE.—THE CHAIRMAN ON THE ESTIMATES. The minutes of the Finance Committee stated, that owing to the accountant having reported that he had been unable to obtain payment of certain menufacturers' accounts, it was resolved that he be authorised to continue the supplies until the next meeting of the committee, on being paid by each of the consumers £lO per week in advance. A deputa- tion from the St. Helens and Sutton Victoria Building Society, had had an interview with the committee in respect to apportionments of sewerage expenses claimed from them. Recommended that the Board remit the apportioned charge, amounting to £l9 ss. Bd. for sewerage expenses in respect of the United Methodist Free Church, Oakland-street, pureuant to section 151 of the Public Health Act, 1875. Resolved that the several committees be requested to prepare estimates for the new General District Rate forthwith. The auditor's report, presented at the last meeting of the Board, was considered, and the Law-Clerk reported that he had for- warded a preliminary appeal against the Auditor's sur- charges to the Local Government Board, and also prepared the draft of the full appeal in accordance with the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875. Resolved that the Law- Clerk's proceedings be approved. Mr. Heves moved, and Mr. GASKELL seconded, the adop- tion of the minutes, which were passed. The CHAIRMAN expressed a hope that in preparing the estimates for the coming year, the various committees would take into consideration the present state of the town, and make their calls as small as they possibly could, consistent with efficiency. ANNUAL TOUR OF INSPECTION. It was unanimously agreed that the members should make their annual inspection of the works of the Board on the 17th inst. This terminated the business.

NEWTON AND FAELISTOWN. EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN SUNDAY Scifoot..—On Sunday last the annual sermons in behalf of the above school were preached, morning and evening, in the Wesleyan Chapel, by the Rev. Walter Vercoe, of Stockport. In the afternoon an address to parents and scholars was delivered by Mr. W. N. Roperoft, of Rainhill. Appropriate hymns were sung during the services by thechildren. The attendance through- out was very good. The total receipts for the day amounted gto £4B 154. Did. CHURCH PARADE AT NEWTON.—The annual church --parade of the C troop Lancashire Hussars and the Newton company of the Liverpool Pres% Guard, took place at St. Peter's Church on Sunday afternoon. There was a full muster of officers and men. The hand of the Lancashire Hussars, under Mr. T. Batley, played a choice selection of Irinsic. The church was crowded, t! e weather being all that could be desired. An excellentand appropriate sermen was preached by the Rev. W. awn.

The monthly meeting as held on Wednesday afternoon, at the cemetery. Mr. Thomas Norman presided, and there were also present—Messrs. Rhodes, Handley, Marshall, Whittaker, Briscoe, Coleburn, Littler, and Salkeld (secretary.)

MISCELLANEOUS. The interments for the last month were 38, of whom eight were Churchmen, 22 Dissenters, and eight Catholics. The total number of interments since the opening of the ceme- tery was 5,448. THE VICAR'S WISHING BILL. _

The SECRETAILY presented a bill from one Ann Ford against the Board for Bs. Bd., including Sc. for washing two surplices. He said that since the question had been referred to at the vestry meeting he had carefully considered the law on the subject. He read a note by W. Cunningham Glen on 15 and 16 Vic., cap. 85, which stated that there was nothing in the Burials Acts which required the Board to pro- vide for the use of the minister performing the Burial Ser- vice in the consecrated part of the burial ground, a surplice or book containing the Burial Service according to the Church of England. These were articles which the parishioners were bound to provide in like manner as other ornaments for the church. Mr. Salkeld went on to say that he supposed that as the cemetery was part of the Parish Church yard the Board ought to provide surplices and a

book of prayers for the minister. - Mr. HANDLEY maintained that the Secretary had altogether misapprehended the distinct meaning of the section, which said that these things were to be provided by the parishioners. Mr. RHODES: But who are the parishioners? Mr. COLEBUTtN: It is a matter for the parishioners' meet- ing to consider on Easter Mondays. The Burial Board have no power. After a desultory conversation, it was decided that, seeing the Burial Board had no power to provide surplices, or pay for the washing of them, the payment should, in future, be discontinued. It was also agreed that as the account of 3s. had been con- tracted before the last meeting of ratepayers was held, it should, under the circumstances, be discharged. Mr. MARSHALL wished to know whether it would be advisable to send a polite message to the Vicar of Runcorn, telling him to get his own surplices washed. (Laughter.) Mr. LrrTLER : The easiest way for the clergy to get out of the difficulty, would be for them not to wear surplices. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. BRISCOE: But that is not the law; let them please themselves—we have nothing to do with that. THE BURIAL FEES QUESTION.

The following letter was read from Mr. Linaker : " Frodsham, 27th April. 1881.—Ruw0rn Union—Dear At a meeting of the Guardians of the Runcorn Union, held on the 19th instant, your letters were read dated the 13th and 18th instants, in reference to the burial of paupers in conse- crated or unconsecrated ground, and the payment of fees there for, when, after a long discussion, it was 'Resolved that the Guardians enter into an agreement with the Runcorn Burial Board, under 18 and 19 Vic., c. 79. sec. 2. for the burial of poor persons in the Runcorn Cemetery.' Will you kindly inform me on what terms the Board will agree with the Guardians for the burial of poor persons In the cemetery, including all tees payable for interment.—l am, yours truly, H. LINAKER Balkeld, Esq., secretary, Burial Board, Runcorn." It was unanimously decided, on the motion of Mr. HAND- LEY, seconded by Mr. MARSHALL, that the Board should enter into a contract with the Guardians for the burial of poor persons in the cemetery, in accordance with the tables of fees provided. Some discussion arose upon the Secretary stating that in the case of boatmen who traded between Runcorn and Manchester, for instance, he had considered that they were engaged in helping to build up the prosperity of the town, and in case of a death in any of their families, he had only charged them single fees for burial. If treated as nos- ratepayers he should have to charge them double fees. Mr. COLEBURN contended that boat people were not resi- dents within the meaning of the Act, and they ought to pay double fees. Mr. MARSHALL thought they ought to abide by the regu- lations of the Act as to charging double fees in such a case. Mr. RHODES considered that such a regulation would nress hardly upon a class of people who were least able to pay double fees. The boat people traded with Runcorn, and spent their money in the town. The CHAIRMAN : YES, but the regulations are against chatging only single fees. Mr. RHODES: The secretary seems to have taken a sensi- ble and humane view of the case. The discussion then dropped, on the understanding that boatpeople would be charged double fees in case of future funerals.

manager at the works, said he asked the defendant why he I put the damper in the flue, and he said, For my own advantage," but he would make no reply to further ques- tions which be put to him upon the subject. He told Little that it was the meanest thing he had ever seen done in the works. Witness also gave a technical explanation of the various items forming the compensation claimed, and the manner in which damaging the draught of the furnace affected the black ash, or the particular chemical con- stituents of which it was composed —Mr. Thomas Glover, chemist, having given evidence, Joseph Ashton, labourer, was put in the box, and distinctly swore that be saw the defendant put in the false damper on the morning of the 26th ult., previous to leaving work, and pull it out before commencing his own turn the next day. Whilst Little was at work the damper was reared against the wall.—Mr. Beasley, for the defence, simply contended that though he did not dispute the fact that the witnesses called on the part of the complainants had stated that which they believed to be true, they were under false impressions as to what really occurred. He called the defendant, who denied hav- ing tampered with the flue, and said it was not true that he ever admitted to Mr. Mcllwaine that he had done so.—The Chairman said the Bench were satisfied that the defendant did insert the false damper, and they assessed the damage which the firm had sustained at £3 3s. It was admitted that the sum of £3 3s. was due to defendant for wages, and this amount would be absorbed by the compensation awarded. Defendants claim for lieu of notice would be dis- missed, and he would have to pay the costs.:
