TUESDAY.—Before Aldermen Webster, and Holmes, and Major Cartwright. Wrmacrr A NAME.—John Horton was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Bewsey, on the previous day, and also with assaulting P.C. Taylor. Prisoner, who appeared to be suffering from delirium tremens, immediately on his name being called, jumped up from his seat and shonted out "That's not my name. I haven't got one. I don't owe you anything. You'll get no name from me." Prisoner then again sat down and was allowed to remain as the Bench thought him unfit to be put in the box.—P.C. Taylor said that on the previous day prisoner was at No. 2, sheet mill, Bewsev ironworks creating a disturbance. He was drunk and was "blackguarding" the workmen. Witness removed prisoner to the ledge and lie then struck him on the face with his fist and kicked him on the leg. With the assistance of a workman he was brought to the police station. In reply to Major Cartwright, Mr. Bunt said he thought prisoner's condition was due to drink. The Bench remanded the prisoner for 48 hours, and instructed Mr. Hunt to keep a watch on him. THE BENCH AND THE MlLlTlA.—William Ford, a militia- man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dial- street the previous night, and also with stealing from the shop of Joseph Crocker, furniture dealer, Dial-street, a brush of the value of is. Pd.—At about eight o'clock on Monday evening, Mrs. Crocker saw a number of militiamen coming up the street and she took her children into the kitchen. Prisoner went into the shop, seized a washing machine and dragged it into the street. Mrs. Crocker seeing the prisoner and a number of other militiamen were drunk, was afraid to interfere with, the prisoner, and she sent for assistance. At this point a man named Miller, who was passing, remonstrated with the prisoner, who then got hold of a chair and a number of other articles, which be threw to the ground, and damaged He at length walked away with a sweeping brush in his possession, and Mrs. Crocker followed him and asked him to return it, but he refused. She went for a constable, and I when she returned found the brush had been thrown into the shop. PC. Lawrence apprehended the prisoner, who resisted "with all his might," and he had to be carried to the police station. Prisoner was very violent in the cells during the whole of the night, and his shoes had to be taken from him —ln reply to Major Cartwright, prisoner said he I came from St. Helens.—Major Cartwright: And it's a pity hut what you had stayed there.—Sergeant Topham gave the prisoner a good character, and said he had been in the militia over four years.—Major Cartwright (to prisoner): It takes our officers one-half their time to look after you fellows. Yon come here and thiek you can do what you like; that's about it. I wish you had been billeted ten miles off. You give our officers more trouble than any other class of men, and we have some bad ones in Warrington.— Prisoner was committed to gaol far fourteen days on each charge. A MIDNIGHT ROW.-'--SAYAGE ASSAULT ON ho WOMAN.— Albert Tomkins, forgeman, was charged with unlawfully assaulting and beating Mary Jane Crosby, a married woman. ' —Mr. Moore appeared for prisoner.—lt appeared that the parties reside near to each other in Pitt-street, off Bewsey- road, and on Saturday night, about eleven o'clock, prosecu- trix was standing in an entry watching for her father's return from the market, when the prisoner came up and abused her in the most brutal manner. Prisoner's wife, father, mother, and sister, then came on the scene, and according to complainant's account they were all striking her at once. The father had his hands on her throat, the sister had hold of her hair, and the others,were striking with their fists and kicking with their feet. A person went to her assistance and released her, bat prisoner was not "satisfied," and struck her with his fist lon the eye, knooking her against a door. had it been a brick wall she "might have been split open." (Laughter.) Complainant's eye was much discoloured. —ln 'cross- ' examination by Mr. Moore, complainant denied having used threatening language to defendant, or having stated that she would "do for him."—Complainant called two witnesses who corroborated her statement.—P.C. Monaghan said he visited complainant's house, and she appeared to have been badly used. Blood was flowing from a wound she had received on her face and her eye was much swollen.—Mr. Moore, having addressed the Bench for the defence, Emma Makin, pri- soner's sister, was called, and she stated complainant threw a quantity of beer upon prisoner, sad struck him on the head with a can, which she took off a woman named Openshaw. She called him a " wastrel " and said she would be "the death of him." P.C. Taylor deposed that when he was going home on the night in question ahead 1130, he heard the complainant, talking very loudly with a large crowd round her. She was uttering threats against the prisoner, and using very filthy language. He got held of her, and told her if she did not go home be should lock her up, but she defird him and he put her into her house. He said there was a disturbance at complainant's house once a week.—The father of the prisoner stated that what he did was in self defence, as prosecutor got hold of his face with her band, taking out two pieces of flesh.—Major Cartwright said it must have been a very savage blow to mark prosecatrix's eye in that

manner, and there was no dOvibt she had been badly abused. —The Bench were of opinion that it had been an aggravated assault, and fined the prisoner 40s. and costs, or in detault a month's imprisonment. WEDNESDAY.—Before Aldermen Davies and Chandley. ROBBERY BY MILITIAMEN.—John Price, alias airmen, of Widnes, and Thomas Hiram, collier, of Wigan, militia- men, were charged with stealing from the shop of John Porter, fishmonger, Buttermarket-street, Warrington, a 1 mackerel, value 6d.—From the statement of Mr. Hunt it ap-1 pearecithat the prisoners were absent from parade on the previous morning without leave. About half-past eleven the prisoners were passing prosecutor's shop window, when Price was seen by a girl named Ann Conner to take from the marble slab a large mackerel. Price handed the fish to Hiram, and the girl then shouted out, " 11l tell that you are taking that fish." Hiram ran after the girl, who had a child in her arms, and she went into the shop of Mr. Can- trell for protection. He followed her in, and said, "I'll kick your guts in. You should not tell tales out of school; shut your mouth." "Then," answered the girl "you should not take fish that doesn't belong to you." The man then stated that he had not stolen the fish. "But," said the girl," you have it in your hand, anyhow." The prisoner Hiram then went away and joined Price, the two going up Cropper's Brow. The girl informed Mrs. Porter of the robbery, and information was given to the police. Evidence having, been given in support of the Chief Constable's statement, P.C. Bowen deposed to apprehending the prisoners, who, when charged, stated they had not been out of the house since ten o'clock, and had never seen any mackerel.—Price pleaded guilty to the charge, but Hiram stated that Price had givtn him the mackerel, telling him he had bought it.--Alderman Davies remarked that though the article stolen was of but small value, the circumstances were such that they would be obliged to deal severely with the case, and prisoners were each sentenced to a month's imprisonment. L THEFT or A BRICKLAYER'S Toots.—Henry Caldwell, a middle-aged man, was charged with stealing from the premises of Shaw Thewlis, about seven o'clock on Saturday evening, one bricklayer's trowel, hammer, and line, the pro- perty of George Cooper, of Mill-lane, Stockton Heath. —Prisoner pleaded guilty.—The prosecutor and his son it appeared had been building a wall at Latchford, and on Saturday noon on leaving work, left their tools lb the hause previously named. About seven o'clock the prisoner went to the house, and by representing that he had been sent for the tools, obtained possession of them from a man named Samuel Ball. He subsequently pledged the trowel and ham- mer at Mrs. Jackson's, pawnbroker, Church-street, for the sum cl Is. 5d., but the police had been unable to recover the line.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for one mouth with hard labour. ALLEGED DESERTION OF FAMILY.—Wm. Dutton, iron- worker, was charged under a warrant with having on the 1 6th February, 1880, unlawfully run away from the town, 1 leaving two children chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—The prisoner was remanded until Friday to give the Guardians an opportunity of sustaining the charge. FRlDAY—Before Captain Reynolds and Mr. John White. DESERTING HIS FAMlLY.—William Dutton, was charged on remand, with deserting two children and leaving them chargeable to the common fund of the Union. Mr. Moore appeared for defendant who pleaded guilty. Mr. , Sutton prosecuted on behalf of the Guardians. He said the 1 prisoner about 15 months ago deserted his wife and four children in consequence of which two of them became in- mates of, the Workhouse. £29 15s. Bd. had been expended on their maintenance. The police bad been very diligent in their exertions to secure the prisoner, but it was not until a day or two ago that he came to Warrington, and on P.C. Berry visiting the house, he found prisoner on the roof of the house in his shirt. The prisoner's conduct was most wrong and unjust and he asked the Bench to takes serious view of the case and inflict the full penalty.—Mr. Moore said he had known the family for many years, and he appeared on be- half of the prisoner as an act of charity. He spoke of the respectibility of prisoner's family, and stated that the reason he left the town was to go in search of work, as he had been discharged from Smethurst's ironworks through slackness in trade. He was willing to pay to the Guardians all money expended in relieving his children.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for two months with hard labour. FRAUDULENT ENLISTMENT.—CharIes Harper, a fine- looking young fellow, was charged with having, on the 23rd April, in the borough of Warrington, unlawfully made a false answer on being attested bcfore a magistrate whilst enlisting in the 2nd Regiment.—Provost Sergeant Cam- bridge said the prisoner answered that he had never previ- ously served in any of Her Majesty's regiments, whereas he had been invalided from the Coldstream Guards.—He was committed to prison for 14 days with hard labour. ASSAULT.--James Farrell was charged with committing a breach of the peace on Thursday by assaulting Ann Cud- more.—lt was stated that defendant and complainant's husband were quarrelling, when the complainant came upon the scene, and she was immediately struck twice by the prisoner.—Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs. UNRULY APPRENTICES.—Robert Forbes.an apprentice,was charged under a warrant for having, on Monday, the 2nd , May, made use of threatening language to Nathaniel Six- ' smith.—Prosecutor, foreman for Messrs. Cartwright and Son, said that on the morning in question, between ten and eleven o'clock, the prisoner found fault with the way in which wi;ness was dividing the moulds,and said he deserved a "b smack in the mouth, and he had a mind to give him one" He was in fear from prisoner's conduct. —The Chief Constable shid that he lead had to have police in the neighbourhood every day during the week through the conduct of the prisoner and a number of others.—Major Cartwright said the conduct of the pri- soner for some months had been very bad and he had led others away. On Monday the whole of the apprentices through the prisoner left work and never returned. He was the ringleader, and for the last few weeks they had had to haves police officer at the office during the time they were paying wages in consequence of the prisoner forcing himself upon the premises after being ordered off. Prisoner one day when ordered off by Major Cartwright, challenged him to fight, and said he had as much right there as anybody else. It was impossible to carry on the work with the prisoner at large.—Prisoner stated that on Monday week the apprentices asked Major Cartwright for a half-day holiday, but he walked out of the gates and the appren.ices followed, and then he said they must finish their day's work, which they did about half-past three. He said he had never given a wrong word.—Major Cartwright said the in i- soner had told P.C. Chantler that he would make it worse for them this summer than last.—As there was no evidence , to corroborate the foreman's statement the case was put in I abeyance for a short time, and at a later period a man I named Herbert Groves proved the threats —ln answer to prisoner, witness said he was not drunk on the morning when the language complained of was used—Prisoner: I reckon he has given von a glass now to square it? Witness: No. —Prisoner : They dursent go against the master or they would be sacked. Major Cartwright : Every man knows that if he does his work properly and conducts him- self properly he has nothing to fear.—Prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO, and two sureties in £5, or in default a month's imprisonment.— Seven apprentices named Alfred Groves, Thomas Potts, William and John Gleave, David Smith, Daniel Ingham, and Thomas Swift were charged with having on the 9th inst. unlawfully conspired together to disobey certain orders of the magistrates, whereby they were required to fulfil their contract with Messrs. C. H. Curtwright and Son.—'S he first two defendants on the list did not put in an appearance, and a warrant was granted for their apprehension.—Major Cart- wright said that on the morning of the 4th inst. the defen- dants went into the works and then walked out again and stayed away the whole of the day. The next morning they were called, but never appeared, and they positively refused , to work. They knew they were putting the firm to very I serious inconvenience and loss by so doing. The work they I had sent out for some months had been very had and since their disappearance there had been a marked improvement. 1 A short time ago the firui had a foreman whom they thought encouraged them, and so they discharged him, and obtained a fresh one, who since his arrival had been in fear through, their threats. If he opened his mouth to them they made I use of oaths. They were complete masters of the whole, place. He was determined to put a stop to this kind of work,l anti he asked the Bench to deal with them in such a way 1 that the firm might conduct their business as well 38,1 other people. The Bench must be aware of the trouble and I anxiety he had had, and the serious losses the firm bad sus- tained through the conduct of the defendants.—Nathaniel Sixsmith confirmed Major Cartwright's statement. The reason they gave him for stopping work was because Major Cartwright bad stopped Forbes. He had given Swift on one occasion 3d. to go back to his work.—The yard.foreman said the conduct of the boys was fearful, and especially to anyone who had a little authority over them.—Defendant William (Heave said he only drew 2s. for the week ending Good Friday, and he ought to have had 10s. He had only received Is. Bd, last week, and that was the reason why he had gone away.—Defendant John (Heave said a fortnight last Saturday. he received only 7d., having 45.10 d, stopped out of his wages.—Captain Reynolds: Why was it stopped? Defendant: For bad work.—the foreman stated that one week there were 1,630 dozen bad bottles through defen- dants' conduct.—The summons against Jahn (Shave was withdrawn on his promising to go Jback to his work and behave himself properly, and pay the costs, 45. Gd. He pro- mised to do this. All the other defendants were committed to gaol for one month. The sentenco MIS afterwards re- voked on the application of the parents, and the Bench im- posed a fine of 30s. and 6s. 6d. costs in each case. FUSTIAN CUTTERS AND THEIR WOREPEOFLE.—Thomas Makin and Wm. Jones were summoned to show cause why they should not be committed to prison for disobedience of an order of the court requiring them to fulfil their contract 4with George Aspy, fustian cutter. Defendants were coin- mitted•to prison for 14days.—Gecrke Aspy made a claim of 13s. against Elizabeth Yates, for neglecting and refusing to fulfil her contract. An order was made for is. per week.— A similar order wan made upon Ann Barnes in payment of a claim of 65.—Parick Mahoney was summoned for neglect- ing his work, whereby George Aspy bad sustained a less of las., and Elizabeth Malloney, his wife, was similarly sum- monedufuorfinaishledos! uonfd £golu4est.o workpaitisoannerr4shehradolaenlet . their np 1. di e ce er sw as made for 2s. upon- the husband, and ls.upon the wife.—Ann Birchall was summoned by Ellen Oakes for absenting herself from her work from the lath to the 231 d April, a loss of £1 7s. being sustained. Mr. Moore, who appeared for the defendant, elicited from the complainant that the claim was for four weeks in add'ltion to the time mentioned in the siammcns. She said Has, loss of one w2.ot was 45. 6d. Mr. Moore said he should, advise his client to pay that sum, and, as that was the MI amount complainant the .--Yelleh Truide = order amid claim uudcr, the summons, accordinglY•

div.head: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.

A special meeting of this Board was held in tbe Board room on Thursday evening, when there were present Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Rogers, Simpson, Gibbon, Hall, Holt, Taylor, Richardson, Ridgway (clerk), and Mallard (deputy clerk).

div.head: PAYMENT OF RATES
div.p: THE PAYMENT OF RATES

The CHAIRMAN read some correspondence which had passed between the clerk and Mrs. McKellar, relating to her liability to pay the rates upon a house for the whole year, when she had only occupied it three months. Mr. RICHARDSON I suppose she did not object to pay for the quarter? The CHAIRMAN
: Oh, no.

Mr. RICHARDSON: Very well, suppose Mrs. McKellar pays for the whole of the year, how will she get it back again? I think that has to be considered. Mr. RILL : You are quite right Mi. Richardson, because if the house is not let the money will have to be refunded. It seemed to him a very lax and round about way of doing business to have to take money and then refund it. Even supposing the house was taken, and Mrs. McKellar paid the whole of the rate, how would she have to get it from the incoming tenant? Seeing that nobody liked paying the rates they might demur. The CHAIRMAN said there was no reason why the Board should refund the money if the house was not let. Mr. ROGERS remarked that the law compelled the pay- ment of the rate; but it left the outgoing tenant power to get anything he could from the incoming tenant. If a person occupied a house for three months he rendered him- self liable for the rates for the twelve months. Mr. SIMPSON : It is not a case for us to deal with. It is for the outgoing and incoming tenants. Mr. TAYLOR observed that the rate was collected in some places half yearly. The CLERK said they could not do that as the Board ordered it to be one rate. Mr. TAYLOR: Then we can only go by one hard and fast line. _ .

Mr. HALL: Yes, we can do it at six months. The CHAIRMAN : Then we must have' a six months' rate. The CLKRIC said that as collector of the Board, it was his duty to collect the rate as quickly as possible, and if he did not collect the whole rate he would be surcharged. He should not, of course, risk that. Some further conversation took place and the matter drop— ped.

SCENE BETWEEN MR. ROGERS AND MR. TAYLOR. Mr. TAYLOR questioned the surveyor (Mr. Mort) as to what steps he had taken to open a drain near Mr. Bailey's house, which was causing a nuisance, and it appeared that he had taken no action in the matter. Mr. Taylor, therefore, moved "That Mr. Mort be instructed to open the grid on the road, and if necessary to carry it into the main sewer, which comes from High lane, and also to open the drain that goes across the meadow into the brook." Mr. HALL seconded. Several members stated that the Board had no power in the matter as the drain was on private property, and Mr. Rogers observed that though to stop the nuisance would be pleasing to him, he thought the Board hadbest letthe matter stand. Mr. TAYLOR said he was surprised that a gentleman who had lived at Statham for twelve months should have allowed the nuisance to exist so long, and yet at the present time he was saying that he would take no notice. Mr. ROGERS : Are you speaking to me? Mr. TAYLOR: Yes. Mr. ROGERS: Then you are speaking in ignorance. We have nothing to do with the drain. Mr. TAYLOR: Can we not ask Mr. Dewhurst or Mr. Fox to do-it? Mr. SIMPSON: You never said that before. The CHAIRMAN: You are taking fresh ground on the matter, Mr. Taylor. Mr. ROGERS: You have no right to do it. Mr. TAYLOR: Mr. Dewhurst would never object. Mr. ROGERS said the mannu in which Mr. Taylor had spoken to him was a gross insult, and he was profoundly ignorant. Mr. TAYLOR: A good thing you are not. Mr. ROGERS: Profoundly ignorant. Mr. HALL remarked that they had been going a long way round to get rid of a nuisance, and he thought to go into these nice little points was hardly generous to Mr. Taylor, who was a new member of the Board, and not sufficiently up to the work, but he meant well. MK SIMPSON: There's no doubt about that. You have instructed him a time or two. Mr. HALL: I have never yet held my-self up as his tutor. The resolution was amended as follows, and passed unani- mously :—" That the Board ask permission to open the mouth of the drain behind Mr. Bayley's property at Statham."
PROPOSED SEWAGE SCHEME FOR LYNIM.-IMPORTANT

div.head: DISCUSSION.
div.p: DISCUSSION.

Mr. ROGERS moved "That Mr. George Dutton be engaged to make tracings of a sewer, commencing near Mr. Hall's house, to pass between Statham Pools and to terminate in a plot of ground, the property of Mr. John Jackson, situate on the north side of the pools; also of a sewer connecting with that from the railway station at a point near the house lately occupied by Mr. Briggs, to pass behind Mr. Bayley's house, and to form a junction with the first named sewer on the south side of the pools, and to mark the gradients of the sewers upon the tracings. That the Surveyor to the Board be instructed to make an estimate of the cost of cem- pleting the scheme." Mr. HATA: said he should like to know before any more mone7 was spent on making tracings and levels whether any portion of those already taken would be of any service in this case. Mr. ROGERS replied that there were tracings in possession of the Board as far as Lymm Well, but he did not suppose they would reduce the cost of Mr. Dutton's engagement. Mr. HALL thought it would first be advisable to know whether the scheme was likely to go on, because if not it was unnecessary to take all those tracings. Mr. ROGERS said that with regard to that the Board had been trying to find a way to deal with the sewage for the last twelve years, and they had not yet succeeded. At one time ,El3O was spent in plans, and when the Board came to consider the scheme it was found to be so expensive that they dropped it. Another scheme propounded was to use a system of tanks and pumps and alie the paraphernalia, and DO was thee spent in plane He had heard it stated that that scheme would have cost over 1£3,000. He had gone carefully into the scheme he Ual. now propounding, and it was so efficient and thorough that it would be passed by the most particular engineer. The- cost of the entire scheme, including the purchasing of the bit of land required, would not exceed £5OO. It was the Cheapest and most economical and effective scheme yet proposed. He had laid it before several practical people, and the answer invariably was that it was the only really efficient scheme for the district and no unprejudiced person could object to it. The valley which they had been trying I to use for 12 years was not available without pumpin‘r', and they all knew what that meant. He referred to the .a.dearr- i tage the scheme possessed in the matter of fall, and said it was the "scheme of schemes." The sewage would be driven from the population, and there was not a house between the termination of the sewer and Thelwall, except] the manure works. They would not find another place in the Faroe circumstances, and if anything should happen which would force the sewage off the filtering ground the Tanners would say they were much obliged. Mr. HALL, for the purpose of letting the public see what the Board was really doing, proposed to ask a few questions which would, perhaps, have the effect of doing away with some prejudice which existed against the scheme. [Mr. Rogers: It is pure prejudice.] He supposed Mr. Rogers had departed from one portion of his scheme—that instead of the sewage going back' into the pools it would go into the river. Mr. ROGERS said there was a .two-acre field which would form a most valuable filtering ground. It,was one of the most important parts of the scheme. If in time it was found too small other portions conld be added without throwing away any expense. Mr.lterA, said that during his electioneering campaign be heard a great deal of talk about that bridge it was proposed to erect. He was not in favour of spending a lot of the rate- payers' money, but they had to get rid of this sewage some way or another, and if the people would look at it in that light, he thought they would have no objection tothe bridge being built over the road to carry it away. It was not matter of choice but a. matter of et:impulsion, because tiney had only to wait until scarlet fever broke out again and they Would then be forced to do that which they were now anxious and desirous to do. Mr. ROGERS waS glad Mr. Hail had spoken of that bridge. He gave some figures showing the enormous sums which bad had to be expended in sewerage schemes in other places. and he remarked that he was proposing a scheme which would not cost more than £500.. With reference to. the bridge, he was desirous of meeting the case fairly, .and he had got another scheme which would. cost about the some as a brick -bridge. He meant a girder bridge, which cold go over the place where it was. required. Ile explained the method by which it could be fixed so as to possess perfect stability. The current at the pools was only four miles an hour, and therefore could not do much damage. Mr. SIMPSON, on Fa being explained that the motion was for the preparation of tracings only, seconded the motion. Mr. fhwr asked if they were not in some way committed to a scheme which had been reported upon by a firm of engineers. The CHAIRMAN replied that they were not. These gentle- men were asked to do certain work with a view to carrying out a sewerage scheme, but it was necessary that they should be paid up to a certain date, and, their account ou.d sent in, it was paid on the understanding that they. sh being sent reckon it as a payment on account of their charges ef they were called in to carry out thee scheme. Mr. ROGERS: We are not compelled to call them in. Mr. HOLT thought it would boa slight upon them not to ask them. Mr. HALL: Do we consider that we paid them a fair re,- Illuneration for what they have done? Mr. HOLT: It N iii part pay ay for the other. payment of the whole scheme, and if we take this we shall have also to p The CLunte said they would 7aOt, The Board had die-.

div.head: MR. RANDLEY ON THE EXISTING MORTGAGES.
div.p: MR. RANDLEY ON THE EXISTING MORTGAGES.

~...... . Mr. HANDLEY brought forward a scheme for the purpose of enabling the Board to utilise the sinking fund in a much better way. He moved the following resolution, which was seconded by Mr. Marshall. and carried unanimously. "That notice be at once given that the three existing mort- gages, at 41 per cent., amounting to £1,700, be paid off in December next. That the Board pay off the sum of £l9O out of the Sinking Fund, and that the balance of £1,510, or thereabouts, be borrowed in sums of £lOO each, at 4 per cent interest, for periods (which will be named in the mort- gage deeds), ranging from one to 13 years." NEW PRECEPT. .
The Board agreed to the issuing, of a precept on the overseers for the sum of £l2O, in order to meet the current expenses. ----•
THE MORTUARY.
It was stated that th—i-s-buildinr;,:-Was on the point of corn-
pletion. The other business before the Board was of a forma character.'
